questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman reports several months of intermittent blurred vision and limb weakness. MRI of the brain shows scattered demyelinating lesions, and her own immune cells are found to be attacking the myelin of her central nervous system. This process best illustrates a failure of which normal property of the immune system?

explanation.summary: Autoimmune disease results when the immune system loses tolerance and attacks the body's own cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines immune tolerance as unresponsiveness to the body's own cells and molecules. When this tolerance is lost, the immune system attacks self-tissue, producing autoimmune disease; the brick specifically names multiple sclerosis as an example in which self-reactivity damages tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonal expansion is the proliferation of an activated lymphocyte into a clone bearing the same receptor; it is a normal effector step, not the property that fails in autoimmunity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematopoiesis is the production of blood cells in the bone marrow and is unrelated to self/non-self discrimination.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization is the antibody- or complement-mediated coating of pathogens to enhance phagocytosis, not a mechanism of self-tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phagocytosis is the engulfment of pathogens and debris by cells such as macrophages and neutrophils; it is an effector function, not the failed regulatory property.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old construction worker sustained a deep implement injury to the leg two days ago. The wound was cleaned and sutured. On follow-up, the redness has resolved and drainage has stopped as the wound closes. During this repair phase, which cell type is chiefly responsible for rebuilding the damaged tissue?

explanation.summary: Tissue repair, the third major function of the immune system, is carried out largely by fibroblasts and endothelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes tissue repair as the immune system's third function: when tissue is damaged, cells rush in, clear the debris, and then fibroblasts and endothelial cells secrete proteins that guide the rebuilding process to restore the tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes kill virus-infected and malignant cells; they do not rebuild damaged tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural killer cells destroy virus-infected, irreparably damaged, and cancerous cells rather than reconstructing tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are early phagocytes that clear microbes and debris but do not carry out the rebuilding of tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies, a humoral defense function, not a repair function.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant has had repeated severe viral and fungal infections. Laboratory studies show a near-absence of mature T lymphocytes, whereas B lymphocytes and antibody levels are relatively preserved. Failure of which structure would best account for the specific lack of mature T cells?

explanation.summary: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that T cells develop in the bone marrow but mature in the thymus, the second of the two primary (generative) lymphoid organs. Absent thymic maturation, mature T cells fail to appear while B-cell development in the marrow can proceed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow generates all immune cells and is where B cells mature; T cells only originate there before migrating to the thymus, so marrow failure would broadly reduce all lineages, not selectively T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature B and T cells encounter antigen, not where T cells are generated or matured.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature B and T cells respond to blood-borne antigen; it is not a site of T-cell maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tonsils are secondary lymphoid tissue (part of the mucosa-associated system) and do not mature T cells.

questions.stem: A researcher studies a marrow-derived cell that gives rise to both the myeloid and lymphoid lineages, ultimately producing all of the cells of the immune system. Which cell is being described?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Memory T cell in the blood

explanation.summary: Hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow give rise to the myeloid and lymphoid lineages.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that hematopoiesis in the bone marrow begins with pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), which differentiate into the myeloid and lymphoid lineages and thereby produce all immune cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A macrophage is a differentiated phagocyte derived from a monocyte and cannot generate the immune lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A megakaryocyte is a committed myeloid cell that produces platelets and does not give rise to lymphoid cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A memory T cell is a long-lived product of an adaptive response, not a precursor of the myeloid and lymphoid lineages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A plasma cell is a terminally differentiated B cell that secretes antibodies; it does not give rise to other lineages.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man develops a rapidly enlarging, painful skin abscess two days after a puncture wound. Aspiration yields thick pus. The predominant cell in this early pus is a short-lived phagocyte that is also a granulocyte and is typically the first to arrive at a site of inflammation. Which cell is it?

explanation.summary: Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes that are the first responders to inflammation and are short-lived.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the neutrophil as a phagocytic granulocyte that ingests and destroys microbes, is generally first on the scene at an area of inflammation, but survives for only a few hours in tissues, making it uniquely both granulocyte and phagocyte in this vignette.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are granulocytes but are involved in allergic reactions and are not phagocytic first responders.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are granulocytes, but they specialize in defense against parasites and hypersensitivity reactions rather than acute pyogenic responses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphocytes are part of the adaptive response and are neither granulocytes nor primary phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophages are phagocytes but are not granulocytes, and they are longer-lived tissue cells rather than the short-lived first responders here.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops hives, wheezing, and hypotension within minutes of a bee sting. The reaction is triggered by IgE antibodies bound to a tissue-resident cell that degranulates, releasing histamine, tryptase, and leukotrienes. Which cell is chiefly responsible?

explanation.summary: Mast cells are IgE-activated tissue cells that release histamine, tryptase, and leukotrienes in hypersensitivity reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the mast cell as a tissue cell involved in tissue repair and in hypersensitivity reactions that, when activated by IgE antibodies or other factors, releases mediators including histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase, matching this immediate allergic reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes kill virus-infected and malignant cells using perforin and granzymes; they do not degranulate to release histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages phagocytose pathogens and present antigen; they are not the IgE-triggered histamine-releasing cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells kill abnormal cells and do not mediate IgE-driven histamine release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells secrete antibodies (including IgE) but do not themselves degranulate to release histamine.

questions.stem: A virus-infected cell is destroyed by a lymphocyte that lacks antigen-specific receptors and instead recognizes the infected and stressed cell directly, inducing apoptosis through perforin and granzymes. Which cell mediates this killing?

explanation.summary: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and abnormal cells without antigen-specific receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the natural killer (NK) cell as an innate lymphoid cell that does not have antigen receptors yet can recognize virus-infected, irreparably damaged, and cancerous cells. Like cytotoxic T cells, NK cells release perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis in their targets.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes carry an antigen-specific B-cell receptor and act through antibodies, not perforin-mediated killing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes do use perforin and granzymes, but they possess antigen-specific, MHC-restricted T-cell receptors, which the stem explicitly excludes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helper T cells use an antigen-specific T-cell receptor and secrete cytokines to direct other cells; they do not kill target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and have no cytotoxic killing function.

questions.stem: Innate immune cells detect conserved microbial structures such as peptidoglycan, but they cannot tell one bacterial species from another. The receptors responsible for this broad, non-specific detection are best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Pattern recognition receptors bind conserved PAMPs and DAMPs but cannot distinguish between pathogen species.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that the receptors of the innate immune system are pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), which bind pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) shared among many pathogens. PRRs can recognize peptidoglycan but cannot distinguish peptidoglycan from different bacterial species.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B-cell receptors bind a single specific antigen with high specificity and can distinguish among closely related strains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MHC class I molecules present peptides to cytotoxic T cells; they are not innate pattern-recognition receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secreted antibodies are highly specific adaptive products, capable of distinguishing between different strains of a pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T-cell receptors are highly specific, MHC-restricted antigen receptors of the adaptive system, not broad pattern detectors.

questions.stem: Human tears and saliva contain an enzyme that helps prevent infection by breaking down peptidoglycan, a critical component of the bacterial cell wall. Which of the following is this enzyme?

explanation.summary: Lysozyme is a barrier antimicrobial enzyme that degrades bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists lysozyme among the antimicrobial chemicals found in secretions such as tears and saliva, describing it as an enzyme that breaks down peptidoglycan, a critical component of the cell wall of many bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3b is a complement opsonin that tags pathogens; it is not the peptidoglycan-degrading enzyme described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defensins are cationic peptides that lyse microbes by forming pores in their membranes, not by enzymatically degrading the cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactoferrin is a barrier protein that binds iron to deprive bacteria of a needed nutrient, not an enzyme that cleaves peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin is a cytotoxic mediator released by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, not a barrier enzyme in tears or saliva.

questions.stem: A soluble arm of innate immunity consists of a complex cascading network of plasma proteins that can directly attack certain pathogens and enhance their clearance. Which of the following is being described?

explanation.summary: The complement system is a cascading network of soluble proteins that directly attacks pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies the complement system as the soluble component of innate immunity, describing it as a complex cascading network of proteins that can directly attack certain pathogens, distinguishing it from the cellular and receptor-based components.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen receptors are membrane-bound recognition molecules of adaptive lymphocytes, not a soluble innate cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytokines are signaling molecules that coordinate immune cells; they are not a cascading protein network that lyses pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defensins are individual antimicrobial peptides of the physical barrier, not a cascading plasma-protein system.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pattern recognition receptors are cell-associated innate receptors, not the soluble complement cascade.

questions.stem: During recovery from a bacterial infection, a patient's serum contains proteins that coat the surface of the bacteria so that phagocytes engulf them more efficiently; these proteins also help trigger the complement cascade but cannot cross cell membranes to reach intracellular pathogens. Which cell produces these proteins?

explanation.summary: Antibodies, which opsonize pathogens and activate complement extracellularly, are produced by plasma cells derived from B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that in humoral immunity, B cells differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies. Antibodies help destroy pathogens by binding their surface and initiating the complement cascade, and they opsonize pathogens to make them easier for phagocytes to eat. Because antibodies act on extracellular pathogens and cannot cross cell membranes, they fit this description.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T lymphocytes kill infected cells directly and do not secrete antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helper T cells secrete cytokines to regulate other immune cells; they do not produce antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural killer cells kill abnormal cells and do not produce antibodies.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are phagocytes that ingest opsonized pathogens but do not manufacture antibodies.

questions.stem: A cell infected with a virus displays viral peptides bound to MHC class I molecules on its surface. Which of the following cells is specifically activated to recognize this display and kill the infected cell using perforin and granzymes?

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic T cells recognize peptides on MHC class I and kill infected or malignant cells with perforin and granzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) recognize peptides presented on MHC class I receptors; once activated, CTLs release perforin and granzymes and primarily attack malignant cells and cells infected by viruses, exactly the scenario described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes bind free antigen through their B-cell receptor and are not MHC class I-restricted killers.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helper T cells recognize peptides on MHC class II presented by antigen-presenting cells and secrete cytokines; they do not directly kill via MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are innate phagocytes and do not perform MHC-restricted killing of infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and have no cytotoxic activity against MHC class I-bearing target cells.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history is evaluated for a chronic cough. Over decades, carcinogens in tobacco smoke have caused mutations to accumulate in his bronchial epithelial cells, yet no tumor has developed because cells that began to look abnormal were destroyed before they could take over healthy tissue. This protection is an example of which major function of the immune system?

explanation.summary: The immune system's second major function is to destroy the body's own cells that have become malignant.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes three functions of the immune system. The second is defense against malignant cells: carcinogens cause mutations to accumulate in healthy cells, and when cells look abnormal the immune system destroys them before they can take over healthy tissue. This is the function protecting the patient in the vignette.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pathogens are microbes capable of causing disease; mutated self cells are not microbes, so this scenario is not the pathogen-defense function.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal flora are non-pathogenic resident bacteria on physical barriers; maintaining them is not a function of the immune system described by the brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukocyte production (hematopoiesis) occurs in the bone marrow and is not one of the three major functions the brick lists for the immune system.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue repair is the third function, in which immune cells clear debris and promote proliferation of fibroblasts and endothelial cells; no tissue damage is being rebuilt here.

questions.stem: A pathologist examining a lung specimen notes organized collections of secondary lymphoid tissue within the mucosa of a large airway. Which of the following is the most specific name for this tissue?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mediastinal lymph node draining the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymus (primary lymphoid organ for T cells)

explanation.summary: Mucosal lymphoid collections are named by location; the lung's subset of MALT is BALT.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that respiratory, GI, and gastroduodenal mucosae contain secondary lymphoid tissue collections called mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), and that subsets of MALT are named by location: gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) of the intestines and bronchi-associated lymphoid tissue (BALT) of the lungs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GALT is the MALT subset of the intestines, not the lungs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymph nodes are discrete secondary lymphoid organs rather than mucosa-associated tissue collections.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen is a discrete secondary lymphoid organ, not a lymphoid collection within the bronchial mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T cells mature; it is not a mucosal lymphoid collection.

questions.stem: An experimental toxin selectively destroys lymphoid progenitor cells in the bone marrow while sparing myeloid progenitor cells. Which of the following cell types would be expected to be absent?

explanation.summary: Natural killer cells, along with B and T lymphocytes, arise from the lymphoid progenitor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that lymphoid cells come from lymphoid progenitor cells and include natural killer (NK) cells as well as B and T lymphocytes. Even though NK cells function as part of the innate immune system, they are lymphoid in origin and would be lost if the lymphoid progenitor were destroyed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophils are myeloid granulocytes and would still be produced.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythrocytes arise from the myeloid progenitor, which is spared by the toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Megakaryocytes are myeloid-lineage cells that give rise to platelets; they are spared.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes come from the myeloid progenitor and would be unaffected.

questions.stem: During an acute bacterial infection of the skin, a circulating phagocyte is signaled by inflammatory mediators to exit the blood vessel and enter the infected tissue, where it differentiates into a macrophage. Which cell is being described?

explanation.summary: Monocytes are circulating phagocytes that serve as macrophage precursors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 of the brick describes the monocyte as a circulating phagocyte that is a macrophage precursor; when signaled by inflammatory mediators to exit blood vessels and enter tissue, monocytes differentiate into macrophages. Figure 1 likewise shows monocytes giving rise to macrophages and dendritic cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are circulating granulocytes involved in allergic reactions and are not macrophage precursors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The dendritic cell is an antigen-presenting cell derived from the monocyte, not the circulating precursor that becomes a macrophage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells are innate lymphoid cells that kill abnormal cells; they are not phagocytes and do not become macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes that are first on the scene but survive only a few hours in tissue; they do not differentiate into macrophages.

questions.stem: A phagocytic cell in the spleen of a healthy 30-year-old man engulfs bacteria, cellular debris, and senescent red blood cells, produces a strong inflammatory response when needed, and also presents antigen to cells of the adaptive immune system. Which cell is it?

explanation.summary: Macrophages are both phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells and clear senescent red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 describes the macrophage as a phagocytic cell and antigen-presenting cell (APC) whose functions include phagocytosis of bacteria, cellular debris, and senescent red blood cells, producing a strong inflammatory response when needed, and interacting with the adaptive immune system as an APC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophils are granulocytes that defend against parasites by releasing major basic protein; they are not phagocytic APCs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells are tissue cells that release histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase; they do not phagocytose senescent red cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells kill virus-infected and cancerous cells with perforin and granzymes; they are neither phagocytes nor antigen presenters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils phagocytose and destroy microbes but are short-lived and are not described as antigen-presenting cells or as clearing senescent red blood cells.

questions.stem: An extracellular bacterial antigen in the skin is taken up by a tissue-resident sentinel cell, processed, and carried to a lymph node, where it is presented to T cells, causing T-cell activation. Which of the following innate immune cells is most specialized for this function?

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells are sentinel antigen-presenting cells that process exogenous antigens and activate T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names dendritic cells among the sentinel cells of the second line of defense, and Table 1 describes the dendritic cell as an antigen-presenting cell whose function is to process and present exogenous antigens to T cells in the adaptive immune system, causing T-cell activation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are circulating granulocytes specialized against parasites and hypersensitivity reactions, not antigen presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells are sentinel cells, but their role is releasing mediators such as histamine, not presenting antigen to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells lack antigen receptors and kill abnormal cells; they do not process and present antigen to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes that ingest and destroy microbes; they are not described as antigen-presenting cells.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy who recently returned from a rural area has abdominal pain, and stool examination shows helminth eggs. A blood smear shows increased numbers of a circulating granulocyte whose granules release major basic protein (helminthotoxin) upon activation. Which cell is it?

explanation.summary: Eosinophils are circulating granulocytes that defend against parasites by releasing major basic protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 describes the eosinophil as a circulating granulocyte that specifically defends against parasitic infections and is involved in hypersensitivity reactions; on activation its granules release histamine, major basic protein (helminthotoxin), and other toxins to aid in the destruction of parasites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are circulating granulocytes involved in allergic reactions whose granules release histamine and heparin, not major basic protein against parasites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells are tissue cells, not circulating cells, and release histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes are circulating phagocytes and macrophage precursors, not granulocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes that ingest and destroy microbes; they are not the parasite-directed cell releasing helminthotoxin.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis has a peripheral blood smear showing increased numbers of a circulating granulocyte whose dark blue-purple granules release histamine and heparin on cell activation. Which cell is it?

explanation.summary: Basophils are circulating granulocytes of allergic reactions whose granules release histamine and heparin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 1 describes the basophil as a circulating granulocyte involved in allergic reactions that contains basophilic granules releasing histamine, heparin, and other mediators on cell activation. The combination of a circulating cell and heparin release distinguishes it from the tissue-resident mast cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are circulating granulocytes, but their granules release major basic protein to destroy parasites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mast cell is a tissue cell, not a circulating cell seen on a blood smear, and its granules release histamine, leukotrienes, and tryptase rather than heparin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes that destroy microbes; they are not the histamine- and heparin-releasing cell of allergic reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies; they are not granulocytes.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman cuts her finger on a kitchen knife. Within moments, before any cells have been recruited from the bloodstream, a tissue-resident cell already stationed in the dermis responds to the breach. Which of the following is such a sentinel cell?

explanation.summary: Sentinel cells are tissue-resident mast cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages that respond immediately to damage or infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes physical barriers as holding areas for sentinel cells, tissue-resident cells that can immediately respond to damage or infection, like sentries patrolling the castle walls. It identifies the sentinel cells of the second line of defense as mast cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages, distinguishing them from circulating cells that come into the area when signaled.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils are circulating granulocytes involved in allergic reactions, not resident sentinel cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are circulating granulocytes, not tissue-resident sentinels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes are circulating phagocytes that enter tissue only when signaled by inflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are generally first on the scene of inflammation, but they arrive from the circulation rather than residing in the tissue beforehand.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man sustains a crush injury to the thigh. Molecules released from his own damaged cells activate natural killer cells and certain pattern recognition receptors. These molecules are best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: DAMPs are molecules released from damaged host cells that activate NK cells and some PRRs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) as molecules released from damage to our own cells. When NK cells recognize DAMPs they can be activated to release perforin and granzymes, and the brick adds that some pattern recognition receptors can also recognize DAMPs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies are secreted B-cell receptors produced by plasma cells; they are not danger signals released from injured tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigens bound by B-cell receptors are recognized by the adaptive immune system with high specificity, not by NK cells and PRRs as danger signals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytokines are signaling molecules that cells actively produce to communicate, not molecules released by cell damage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PAMPs are compounds shared among many pathogens, such as peptidoglycan; they come from microbes, not from the host's own damaged cells.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old unvaccinated child is exposed to measles virus for the third time in his life. Compared with the first exposure, the innate immune response to this third exposure is expected to be which of the following?

explanation.summary: The innate immune system has no memory, so its response is identical on every exposure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that innate immune responses are preprogrammed into the genome, so the innate immune response to the measles virus will be exactly the same the second or third time a person is exposed as it is the first time. Table 2 summarizes innate memory as none.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The innate response is present on every exposure; it is the germline-encoded first and second lines of defense.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A faster, stronger response on re-exposure is the memory feature of the adaptive immune system, not the innate system.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antigen specificity belongs to B- and T-cell receptors of the adaptive system; innate PRRs remain nonspecific on every exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nothing in the brick suggests the innate response weakens with repeated exposure; it stays the same.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl who received the measles vaccine at age 12 months is exposed to a classmate with measles. Memory B and T cells generated by the vaccine are rapidly activated. Approximately how quickly does this secondary adaptive immune response occur?

explanation.summary: A secondary adaptive response driven by memory lymphocytes occurs in seconds to hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that on initial exposure (primary immune response) memory B and T cells are made, and on subsequent exposure (secondary immune response) the rapid activation of memory lymphocytes allows a response to occur in seconds to hours. Table 2 lists adaptive timing as weeks for the primary response and seconds to hours for the secondary response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One to two weeks is on the order of the primary adaptive response, which Table 2 lists as taking weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A response within days describes the initial (primary) adaptive response shown in Figure 2, not the memory-driven secondary response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No adaptive response in the brick takes months; the secondary response is nearly as fast as innate immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Several weeks is the primary response timing in Table 2, not the secondary response.

questions.stem: A researcher compares the gene encoding a macrophage's pattern recognition receptor with the gene encoding a T cell's antigen receptor. Which of the following best describes the difference in how these two receptors are generated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both are encoded directly in germline DNA without any rearrangement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both are produced by gene rearrangement, recombination, and hypermutation

choices.label: C
choices.text: The PRR is encoded directly in germline DNA; the TCR is produced by gene rearrangement

choices.label: D
choices.text: The PRR is produced by gene rearrangement; the TCR is encoded directly in germline DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: The PRR is produced by hypermutation; the TCR is encoded directly in germline DNA

explanation.summary: Innate receptors are germline-encoded, whereas adaptive antigen receptors are produced by gene rearrangement, recombination, and hypermutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Table 2 contrasts the genetics of the two systems: innate receptors (PRRs) are encoded directly in germline DNA, which is why innate responses are preprogrammed into the genome, whereas adaptive antigen receptors (T- and B-cell receptors) are produced by gene rearrangement, recombination, and hypermutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only the innate PRR is germline-encoded; the adaptive TCR requires gene rearrangement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only adaptive receptors are produced by rearrangement, recombination, and hypermutation; PRRs are not.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the relationship; it is the TCR, not the PRR, that arises by gene rearrangement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypermutation is a feature of adaptive receptor generation, and the TCR is not germline-encoded.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman develops profuse diarrhea and colitis 10 days after completing a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Stool testing is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin. Loss of which of the following innate defenses best explains her infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acidic pH of the stomach contents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ciliary movement of mucus in the gut lining

choices.label: D
choices.text: Competition by the resident gut microbiota

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lysozyme secretion into the intestinal lumen

explanation.summary: Antibiotics disrupt the protective gut microbiota, allowing C. difficile spores to germinate and produce toxins.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that normal flora compete with pathogens for resources and inhibit their growth. Its clinical correlation states that disruption of the gut microbiota through antibiotic use increases the risk of C. difficile infection: when protective bacteria are diminished, C. difficile spores can germinate and produce toxins that damage the intestinal lining, causing diarrhea and colitis. Fecal microbiota transplantation can help restore microbial balance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stomach's acidic environment is a chemical barrier that antibiotics do not abolish; the brick ties C. difficile to depletion of protective bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The complement cascade is a soluble network of plasma proteins; it is not the barrier defense disrupted by antibiotic use.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cilia are found on cells lining the respiratory and upper gastrointestinal tract, where they move mucus upward; they are not the colonic defense lost here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysozyme is an enzyme in secretions that breaks down peptidoglycan; antibiotics do not remove lysozyme, and the brick attributes C. difficile risk to microbiota loss.

questions.stem: A dermatology resident explains to a student that the surface of healthy skin is chemically unfavorable to most microbes because of its high salt concentration and its pH. Which of the following pH ranges best approximates that of normal skin?

explanation.summary: The skin's low pH of 4.5 to 5.5, together with high salt, makes it unfavorable to most microbes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists chemical features of physical barriers that prevent infection and specifically states that the skin's low pH (4.5-5.5) and high salt concentration make the area unfavorable to most microbes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pH this low corresponds to the highly acidic environment of the stomach into which swallowed mucus is delivered, not to the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A neutral pH would not be the mildly acidic, microbe-unfavorable surface the brick describes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick describes the skin as low in pH, not alkaline.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A strongly alkaline surface is not a feature of skin described anywhere in the brick.

questions.stem: An investigator finds that a bacterial strain requiring abundant iron for growth fails to proliferate when cultured in human saliva. Removing a single protein from the saliva restores bacterial growth. Which of the following is that protein?

explanation.summary: Lactoferrin in secretions binds iron, a critical factor for many bacteria, and thereby limits their growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists three antimicrobial chemicals in mucus, tears, and saliva. The third is lactoferrin, a protein that binds iron, a critical factor for many bacteria. Sequestering iron starves iron-dependent bacteria, matching the experimental observation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement is a cascading network of plasma proteins that attacks pathogens; it is not the iron-binding protein of secretions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defensins are cationic peptides that lyse microbes by forming pores in their cytoplasmic membranes, not by depriving them of iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine is a mediator released from mast cell and basophil granules in hypersensitivity, not an antimicrobial protein in saliva.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysozyme is an enzyme that breaks down peptidoglycan in the bacterial cell wall; it does not act by binding iron.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has had recurrent lower respiratory tract infections since infancy. Evaluation shows that the fine, hair-like protrusions on the surface of her respiratory epithelial cells are immotile. Which of the following protective mechanisms is most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Competition by normal flora for nutrients and binding sites

choices.label: B
choices.text: Emptying of intestinal contents by peristaltic contraction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enzymatic breakdown of bacterial peptidoglycan by lysozyme in tears

choices.label: D
choices.text: Movement of mucus and trapped microbes upward out of the airway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pore formation in microbial membranes by secreted defensins

explanation.summary: Cilia move mucus and anything trapped in it upward so it can be coughed up or swallowed into the acidic stomach.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes cilia as fine, hair-like protrusions on cells lining the respiratory and upper gastrointestinal tract. These cilia move mucus (and anything in it) upward so it can be coughed up or swallowed into the highly acidic environment of the stomach, acting like an elevator for microbes and inhaled particles (Figure 3). Immotile cilia lose this mechanical barrier function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Normal flora competition is a microbiota-based defense, not a function of cilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peristalsis is a mechanical barrier of the intestine and is not performed by respiratory cilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidoglycan breakdown is the chemical action of lysozyme, unrelated to ciliary motion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defensin pore formation is a chemical barrier feature and does not depend on cilia.

questions.stem: A helper T cell is activated only when its T-cell receptor engages a peptide displayed in an MHC class II molecule. Which of the following cells is capable of presenting antigen to this helper T cell?

explanation.summary: MHC class II is expressed only by antigen-presenting cells: B cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that helper T cells recognize peptides on MHC class II receptors, and that MHC II is only expressed by B cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells, collectively called antigen-presenting cells (APCs). APCs internalize and break up extracellular antigens before presenting them on MHC II. Of the choices, only the dendritic cell is an APC.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils are granulocytes that combat parasites and are not antigen-presenting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mast cells release mediators such as histamine and tryptase; they are not among the three APC types.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells lack antigen receptors and kill abnormal cells; they are not MHC II-expressing APCs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are phagocytic granulocytes; the brick does not list them among the MHC II-expressing APCs.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has severe, uncontrolled inflammatory responses affecting multiple organs. Studies show that he lacks a specific subtype of helper T cells whose normal role is to downregulate the immune response. Which cell type is deficient?

explanation.summary: Regulatory T cells are a helper T cell subtype that downregulates the immune response.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a specific type of helper T cells, regulatory T cells, downregulate the immune response, and its summary repeats that regulatory T cells downregulate the immune response as part of cell-mediated immunity. Without them, the tight regulation the brick says the immune system requires is lost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T cells directly attack virus-infected and malignant cells; they are not a helper T subtype and do not downregulate responses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Memory B cells provide rapid antibody responses on re-exposure; they are B cells, not helper T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural killer cells are innate lymphoid cells that kill abnormal cells; they are not T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies, not regulators of the response.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman recovers from an acute bacterial infection. Over the following weeks, the large population of pathogen-specific B and T cells that expanded during the infection shrinks back toward baseline. Which of the following processes accounts for this decline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis of most of the expanded B and T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued clonal expansion of the activated clones

choices.label: C
choices.text: Differentiation of all the cells into plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phagocytosis of the lymphocytes by neutrophils

choices.label: E
choices.text: Return of the lymphocytes to primary lymphoid organs

explanation.summary: Contraction and homeostasis: once an infection is cleared, most generated B and T cells undergo apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the general features of the adaptive immune system, the brick lists contraction and homeostasis: when an infection is cleared, most of the generated B and T cells go through apoptosis. This returns the lymphocyte population toward baseline after the clonal expansion that occurred during the response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonal expansion is the proliferation phase in which an activated clone divides into many child cells; it is the opposite of the contraction described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only B cells become plasma cells, and the brick says most generated cells die by apoptosis rather than persisting as effectors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes contraction to apoptosis of the lymphocytes themselves, not to neutrophil phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary lymphoid organs generate lymphocytes; the brick does not describe effector cells returning there after infection.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man received an influenza vaccine last fall and asks why he needs another one this year, since his immune system should still remember last year's vaccine. Which of the following best explains the need for annual revaccination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: BCRs and TCRs are too nonspecific to distinguish between different influenza strains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza changes its antigens, so last year's memory cells are not specific for this year's strains

choices.label: C
choices.text: Killed or weakened pathogens in vaccines are unable to generate memory B and T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Memory B and T cells generated by vaccination undergo apoptosis within a few months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccine-induced memory resides only in the innate immune system, which lacks lasting memory

explanation.summary: Because BCRs and TCRs are highly strain-specific and influenza changes its antigens, last year's memory cells do not match this year's virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that the specificity of BCRs and TCRs is why there is a new influenza vaccine every year: memory to this year's vaccine persists a year from now, but influenza is very good at changing its antigens, so those memory cells will not be specific for next year's virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCRs and TCRs are highly specific and can distinguish between different influenza strains; that specificity is precisely the reason a new vaccine is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick states that vaccines made of parts of a pathogen, killed pathogen, or weakened pathogen do generate adaptive responses and memory.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick explicitly says the memory from this year's flu vaccine will still be present a year from now; the memory does not disappear.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaccines work through adaptive memory; the innate system has no memory and is not the basis of vaccination.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is infected with a bacterium that has been phagocytosed by his macrophages but continues to live within them. Which of the following adaptive immune mechanisms is chiefly responsible for eliminating this pathogen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies that opsonize the bacterium in the extracellular space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement-mediated lysis of the bacterium in the plasma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells that lyse the macrophage with perforin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helper T cell cytokines that activate the infected macrophage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory T cells that downregulate the inflammatory response

explanation.summary: Phagocytosed microbes living within macrophages are eliminated when helper T cells activate the macrophage.
explanation.whyCorrect: Figure 4 of the brick assigns phagocytosed microbes that can live within macrophages to the helper T lymphocyte, whose effector mechanism is the activated macrophage and whose function is elimination of phagocytosed microbes. The text adds that helper T cells, once activated by peptide and MHC II, release cytokines that enhance the phagocytic ability of macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibodies act on extracellular pathogens because they cannot cross cell membranes; a bacterium inside a macrophage is beyond their reach.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement attacks pathogens in plasma and extracellular space, not bacteria sheltered inside a macrophage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Figure 4 assigns cytotoxic T cells to intracellular microbes such as viruses replicating within infected cells, where they kill the infected cell; the helper T-macrophage axis handles phagocytosed microbes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Regulatory T cells downregulate immune responses; they do not eliminate intracellular bacteria.

questions.stem: During lymphocyte development, a newly generated B or T cell whose antigen receptor reacts against the host's own molecules is destroyed or inactivated. According to the feature of nonreactivity to self, in which location does this elimination occur?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary lymphoid organs, on antigen encounter

explanation.summary: Self-reactive B and T cells are destroyed or inactivated before they leave the primary lymphoid organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the features of the adaptive immune system, the brick lists nonreactivity to self (tolerance): B and T cells that react to the host are destroyed or inactivated before they are released from primary lymphoid organs, that is, the bone marrow and thymus where lymphocytes are generated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MALT is a secondary lymphoid tissue for antigen encounter, not a site of lymphocyte generation and tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma and extracellular space are where humoral immunity acts through antibodies, not where developing lymphocytes are screened.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary lymphoid organs are where mature B and T cells encounter antigens such as toxins and allergens, not where self-reactive cells are eliminated before release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sites of infection are where effector responses occur, not where developing self-reactive lymphocytes are removed.

questions.stem: A 12-month-old infant receives the measles vaccine, which is made of weakened measles virus that can get inside the child's cells. Which of the following best describes how this vaccine protects the child?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It generates an adaptive response and memory without causing measles infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: It induces tolerance so the immune system ignores measles antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: It stimulates normal flora to compete with measles virus for resources

choices.label: D
choices.text: It strengthens the innate immune response to all future measles exposures

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies pre-formed antibodies that persist in the plasma for life

explanation.summary: Vaccines exploit immunologic memory: a weakened pathogen generates an adaptive response and memory without causing the disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation explains that knowledge of immunological memory allowed us to generate vaccines, which expose the immune system to parts of a pathogen, killed pathogen, or weakened pathogen. The measles vaccine is weakened measles virus that can get inside cells, generate an adaptive response, and make memory to measles without the person actually being infected with measles.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Tolerance is unresponsiveness to self; a vaccine does the opposite by generating an active response and memory against the pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Normal flora competition is an innate barrier defense unrelated to how vaccines work.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The innate immune system has no memory; its response is the same on every exposure and cannot be strengthened by vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vaccine contains weakened virus, not antibodies; protection comes from the child's own memory B and T cells.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man in the intensive care unit is being treated for Escherichia coli bacteremia. He develops fever, tachycardia, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane of this gram-negative organism is the key molecule driving his innate response. Which pattern recognition receptor most directly senses this molecule?

explanation.summary: TLR4 is the surface toll-like receptor that recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a component of the cell wall of many gram-negative bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: External toll-like receptors sit on the cell membrane and recognize extracellular bacterial and fungal PAMPs. The brick identifies TLR4 as the most important external TLR, recognizing LPS. Extensive TLR4 activation by high LPS levels is a known driver of the dysregulated, shock-inducing response seen in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TLR2 recognizes bacterial peptidoglycan, not LPS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TLR3 is an internal (endosomal) receptor that detects double-stranded viral RNA, not a bacterial cell-wall component.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TLR5 recognizes flagellin, the protein of bacterial flagella, rather than LPS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLR9 is an endosomal receptor that senses CpG DNA, not surface LPS.

questions.stem: A researcher studies how a cell detects a respiratory virus that has entered its endosomes and released double-stranded RNA. She identifies an internal toll-like receptor located in the membrane of endolysosomes that binds this viral nucleic acid and triggers signaling. Which receptor is she most likely studying?

explanation.summary: Internal toll-like receptors such as TLR3 reside in intracellular vesicles and detect PAMPs of intracellular pathogens like viruses, including double-stranded RNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that internal TLRs are located in the membranes of internal vesicles (endoplasmic reticulum or endolysosomes) and detect PAMPs of pathogens that invade human cells, such as viruses. In the signaling figure, TLR3 is the endosomal receptor paired with double-stranded RNA. Deficiencies of TLR3 are associated with severe herpesvirus infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NOD-like receptors are cytosolic sensors that form inflammasomes; they are not the endosomal double-stranded RNA sensor described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TLR2 is an external, surface receptor for bacterial peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TLR4 is an external surface receptor for LPS, not endosomal double-stranded RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLR5 is a surface receptor for flagellin.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man with chronic granulomatous bowel inflammation is found to carry a mutation in NOD2. This gene encodes a cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that, upon binding intracellular PAMPs, assembles a large multiprotein complex. Activation of this complex most directly drives the production of which pro-inflammatory cytokine?

explanation.summary: NOD-like receptors form inflammasomes, which induce inflammation by producing the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that binding of PAMPs to NLRs induces formation of inflammasomes, large cytosolic multiprotein complexes that induce inflammation through production of pro-inflammatory IL-1. Mutations in NOD2 are specifically associated with chronic inflammatory disorders such as Crohn disease and sarcoidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma is a type II interferon produced mainly by NK and helper T cells; it is not the inflammasome product.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits, rather than drives, inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-8 is a chemokine that recruits neutrophils; it is not produced by inflammasome activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is an anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive cytokine that suppresses immune cells and promotes wound healing.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has severe, early-onset inflammatory bowel disease. Genetic testing reveals loss of function of a cytokine normally produced by macrophages, dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells that inhibits activation of both innate and adaptive immune cells and downregulates MHC expression. Deficiency of which cytokine best explains his condition?

explanation.summary: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine whose deficiency is linked to autoimmunity and inflammatory bowel disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes IL-10 as produced by macrophages, dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells, functioning to inhibit pro-inflammatory cytokines, block innate activation by PAMPs and T-cell activation, and reduce MHC expression. It specifically notes that IL-10 deficiency is associated with autoimmunity and inflammatory diseases such as multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-1 is pro-inflammatory; its loss would reduce, not cause, inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-6 is a pro-inflammatory pyrogen and acute-phase inducer, not an anti-inflammatory regulator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-8 is a neutrophil-recruiting chemokine and does not suppress immune activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is pro-inflammatory; excess, not deficiency, drives inflammatory disease.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is started on etanercept, a fusion protein that acts as a decoy receptor to neutralize a pro-inflammatory cytokine. High levels of this same cytokine can induce shock with hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation, and the drug carries a risk of immunosuppression. Which cytokine does etanercept target?

explanation.summary: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine targeted by anti-TNF biologics such as etanercept, adalimumab, and infliximab.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that because of TNF-alpha's importance in inflammation, monoclonal antibodies (adalimumab, infliximab) and the fusion decoy receptor etanercept are used to treat inflammatory conditions, and that these drugs carry a risk of immunosuppression. It also notes that high levels of TNF-alpha can induce shock, including hypotension and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma activates macrophages and upregulates MHC; it is not targeted by etanercept.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-2 is a T-cell growth/proliferation signal and is not the target of etanercept.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-8 is a neutrophil chemokine, not the cytokine neutralized by anti-TNF therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta is an anti-inflammatory cytokine, not a target for suppression in rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: In an experiment, an investigator applies a compound to inflamed tissue and observes markedly reduced migration of neutrophils from the blood into a site of bacterial infection. The compound most likely blocks the activity of which cytokine?

explanation.summary: IL-8 (CXCL8) is the chemokine that drives neutrophil chemotaxis to sites of inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes IL-8/CXCL8 as a chemokine that recruits neutrophils from the blood into an area of inflammation, enhancing their migration by increasing adhesion molecule expression and anchoring the neutrophil to the endothelium. Blocking IL-8 activity would therefore reduce neutrophil migration to the infected site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory and suppresses immune activation; blocking it would increase inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-2 promotes T-cell proliferation and is not a neutrophil chemoattractant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta suppresses immune cells and promotes wound healing rather than driving neutrophil chemotaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha upregulates adhesion molecules but the chemokine principally responsible for directed neutrophil migration is IL-8.

questions.stem: A cell infected with influenza virus recognizes the pathogen through its pattern recognition receptors and secretes a cytokine into the surrounding tissue. Neighboring cells respond by inducing antiviral enzymes such as RNase L and by increasing surface expression of MHC class I. Which cytokine mediates this response?

explanation.summary: Type I interferons (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta) are produced by virus-infected cells and act in autocrine and paracrine fashion to establish an antiviral state and raise MHC class I.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that type I interferons are produced by virus-infected cells as a result of PRR recognition and act on the infected cell and its neighbors to induce antiviral enzymes; RNase L degrades viral RNA, and other enzymes block translation. It further notes that IFN-alpha and IFN-beta increase MHC class I expression, making it easier for cytotoxic T cells to find and kill infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma is a type II interferon that mainly activates macrophages and upregulates MHC class II; it is produced by NK and helper T cells, not the infected cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-12 helps activate NK cells but does not itself induce the antiviral enzyme response described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-6 is a pyrogen and acute-phase inducer, not an antiviral interferon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine and does not mediate the interferon-driven antiviral state.

questions.stem: During a chronic intracellular infection, NK cells and helper T cells secrete a cytokine that enhances the ability of macrophages to phagocytose and kill pathogens and that upregulates MHC class II expression on antigen-presenting cells. Which cytokine is being described?

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma is the type II interferon that activates macrophages and preferentially upregulates MHC class II.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies IFN-gamma as the main type II interferon, produced primarily by NK cells (innate) and helper T cells (adaptive). It activates macrophages, increasing their ability to phagocytose and kill pathogens, and although it can raise MHC class I, it is more efficient at increasing MHC class II expression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-alpha is a type I interferon produced by virus-infected cells; it establishes an antiviral state rather than acting as the main macrophage activator.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IFN-beta is likewise a type I interferon with antiviral function, not the NK/T-cell-derived macrophage activator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory and actually downregulates MHC expression and immune activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-8 is a chemokine for neutrophil recruitment and does not activate macrophages or upregulate MHC II.

questions.stem: A virus evades detection by cytotoxic T cells by downregulating MHC class I molecules on the surface of the cells it infects. Despite this, the infected cells are still recognized and killed by an innate lymphocyte that lacks antigen receptors. Which cell is responsible for killing these MHC-class-I-low cells?

explanation.summary: NK cells recognize and kill virus-infected cells that have decreased MHC class I, a hallmark of missing-self recognition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that NK cells are lymphocytes that do not express antigen receptors and can recognize a cell infected by a virus when MHC class I is decreased, which many viruses do to evade cytotoxic T cells. Loss of MHC class I removes the NK inhibitory signal, licensing the NK cell to kill the target.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic CD8 T cells require MHC class I to recognize their target; downregulation of MHC class I is exactly how the virus evades them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mast cells release vasoactive mediators such as histamine and are not cytotoxic killers of infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are phagocytes for extracellular microbes and do not perform MHC-based killing of virus-infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells secrete antibodies and do not directly kill infected cells.

questions.stem: A virus-infected cell becomes coated with IgG antibodies directed against a viral surface antigen. An NK cell then binds the Fc portion of these antibodies through a specific surface receptor and kills the coated cell. Which NK-cell receptor mediates this antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity?

explanation.summary: CD16 (FcγRIII) is the NK-cell Fc receptor that binds IgG-coated targets to trigger antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that NK cells have antibody receptors on their surface; when an antibody binds antigens on the surface of infected cells, NK cells kill the target, a process called antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. It specifies that for NK-mediated ADCC, IgG must bind the specific NK receptor CD16.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a costimulatory receptor on T cells, not the NK ADCC receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas is a death receptor on target cells engaged by FasL; it is not the NK receptor that binds IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I is the self-signal NK cells monitor for missing-self recognition; it does not bind antibody Fc.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLR4 is a pattern recognition receptor for LPS, not an antibody Fc receptor.

questions.stem: An NK cell contacts a virus-infected target and releases the contents of its cytolytic granules. One granule protein inserts into the target cell membrane and forms pores, allowing a second class of granule enzymes to enter and cleave caspases, triggering apoptosis. Which protein forms these membrane pores?

explanation.summary: Perforin forms pores in the target membrane, allowing granzymes to enter and induce apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that NK cells can release cytolytic granules containing perforin, which forms pores in cell membranes, and granzymes, which are proteases that cleave caspases to induce apoptotic signaling. The pore-forming protein described is perforin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defensins are antimicrobial peptides that inhibit or kill microbes, not the pore-forming protein of NK granules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granzymes are the proteases that enter through the pores to cleave caspases; they do not form the pores themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactoferrin is an antimicrobial protein that sequesters iron; it does not form membrane pores in target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysozyme is an antimicrobial enzyme that degrades bacterial cell walls, not an NK pore-former.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with lobar pneumonia has a temperature of 39.1 C, heart rate of 112/min, respiratory rate of 24/min, and a leukocyte count of 15,400/mm3. His blood pressure is 122/78 mm Hg and remains stable. Based on the framework presented in this brick, which of the following best classifies his condition?

explanation.summary: Sepsis is defined as SIRS occurring in the presence of a documented infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient meets multiple SIRS criteria (temperature over 38 C, heart rate over 90, respiratory rate over 20, and WBC over 12,000). The brick defines sepsis as SIRS in the presence of an infection; because he has documented pneumonia, his condition is best classified as sepsis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytokine storm names the underlying positive-feedback mechanism of inflammation, not a clinical diagnostic stage on the SIRS-to-MODS spectrum.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MODS requires damage to multiple organ systems beyond septic shock, which is not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Septic shock requires cytokine-induced persistent hypotension despite IV fluids; his blood pressure is normal and stable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SIRS without infection applies to sterile triggers such as trauma or pancreatitis, but this patient has a clear infectious source.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has an acute myocardial infarction. Within hours, neutrophils and macrophages accumulate in the infarcted myocardium even though no microorganisms are present. Pattern recognition receptors on local cells have been activated by molecules released from the dying cardiomyocytes. Which of the following best characterizes the molecules that triggered this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemotactic cytokines named with the prefix CCL or CXCL

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intracellular molecules such as ATP and DNA released by necrotic cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lipid mediators that sensitize nerve endings but do not bind PRRs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Molecules critical to pathogen survival that are absent from human cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Molecules released in a controlled manner by apoptotic cells

explanation.summary: Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) such as DNA and ATP are released by necrotic cells and bind PRRs, signaling that injury rather than normal cell turnover has occurred.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that DAMPs are released by necrotic cells (cells dying in an inflammatory way) but not by apoptotic cells (cells dying in a controlled, non-inflammatory way). When DAMPs bind PRRs, cells know that injury has occurred, and immune cells are recruited even during sterile injuries. DNA and ATP are the brick's examples of DAMPs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemokines are cytokines produced by cells to direct migration; they are not the molecules released from dying cells that bind PRRs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes prostaglandins, which damaged cells secrete to cause pain and encourage inflammation but which do not bind PRRs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This describes PAMPs, which come from pathogens; no microorganism is present in this sterile infarct.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Apoptotic cells die in a controlled, non-inflammatory way and do not release DAMPs.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man cuts his knee while playing football. The next day the wound is exquisitely painful to the touch. Damaged cells at the site have secreted a molecule that sensitizes local nerves and encourages inflammation but does not bind pattern recognition receptors. Which of the following is this molecule?

explanation.summary: Prostaglandins secreted by damaged cells sensitize nerves and cause pain, but unlike DAMPs they do not bind PRRs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that damaged cells can secrete molecules like prostaglandins, which sensitize nerves, cause pain, and encourage inflammation, but do not bind PRRs. In the extracellular response, damage to tissue induces DAMPs and releases prostaglandins, accounting for the pain that is one of the four cardinal signs of inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ATP is a DAMP released by necrotic cells; it binds PRRs rather than directly sensitizing nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-8 is a chemokine that recruits neutrophils; it is a cytokine, not a nerve-sensitizing mediator from damaged cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lipopolysaccharide is a bacterial PAMP that binds TLR4; it is not secreted by damaged human cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zymosan is a fungal PAMP recognized by PRRs, not a product of damaged host cells.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops a skin abscess caused by Staphylococcus aureus, a gram-positive organism. Toll-like receptors on the surface of resident macrophages recognize peptidoglycan in the organism's thick cell wall and activate NF-κB, leading to inflammatory cytokine production. Which receptor most directly recognizes this cell-wall component?

explanation.summary: TLR2 is the external toll-like receptor that recognizes bacterial peptidoglycan.
explanation.whyCorrect: External TLRs on the cell surface recognize mainly bacterial and fungal components such as flagella proteins and peptidoglycan. In the brick's signaling figure, TLR2 is the surface receptor paired with bacterial peptidoglycan, and it signals through NF-κB to drive inflammatory cytokine transcription.

whyWrongByChoice.B: TLR3 is an endosomal receptor for double-stranded viral RNA, not a surface receptor for a bacterial cell-wall component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TLR4 recognizes LPS; in the brick's figure, peptidoglycan is paired with TLR2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TLR7 is an endosomal receptor for single-stranded RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLR9 is an endosomal receptor for CpG DNA.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man is infected with a single-stranded RNA virus. After the virus is taken up into the endosomes of a dendritic cell, a toll-like receptor in the endosomal membrane binds the viral single-stranded RNA and signals through NF-κB. Which receptor is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: TLR7 is the endosomal toll-like receptor that recognizes single-stranded RNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Internal TLRs sit in the membranes of internal vesicles such as endolysosomes and detect PAMPs of pathogens that invade human cells, such as viruses. In the brick's signaling figure, the endosomal receptors are TLR7 (ssRNA), TLR3 (dsRNA), and TLR9 (CpG DNA); TLR7 is the one paired with single-stranded RNA and it signals to NF-κB.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TLR3 is endosomal but recognizes double-stranded RNA, not single-stranded RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TLR4 is a surface receptor for LPS, not an endosomal viral RNA sensor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TLR5 is a surface receptor for flagellin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLR9 is endosomal but recognizes CpG DNA, not RNA.

questions.stem: A research group generates macrophages that lack every member of the IRF transcription factor family, including IRF3 and IRF7, but retain intact NF-κB signaling. The cells are stimulated with lipopolysaccharide through TLR4. Compared with normal macrophages, which of the following responses is most likely to be selectively lost in the mutant cells?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-alpha

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recruitment of adaptor proteins to the receptor

explanation.summary: Downstream PRR signaling uses two major transcription factors: IRFs drive type I interferon production, while NF-κB drives inflammatory cytokine production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PRR signaling involves two major transcription factors, NF-κB and interferon regulatory factors. In the signaling figure, TLR4 activates both: the IRF arm leads to type I IFN, and the NF-κB arm leads to inflammatory cytokines. Cells lacking IRFs but retaining NF-κB would therefore lose type I IFN production while still making inflammatory cytokines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: LPS binding to TLR4 occurs at the receptor itself and is unaffected by loss of a downstream transcription factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Inflammasomes form after NOD-like receptors bind PAMPs; they are not a product of IRF signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inflammatory cytokines are produced through the NF-κB arm, which is intact in these cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adaptor proteins interact with the PRR upstream of both transcription factors; their recruitment does not depend on IRFs.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is hospitalized with his second episode of severe herpes simplex virus encephalitis. He has no history of unusual bacterial or fungal infections. His physician suspects an inherited defect in an innate receptor and orders functional testing and gene sequencing. A deficiency of which of the following receptors is most likely?

explanation.summary: Deficiencies of TLR3 are associated with severe herpesvirus infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that deficiencies of TLR3, an internal TLR that detects viral double-stranded RNA, are associated with severe herpesvirus infections, and that functional testing and gene sequencing of the TLRs can be ordered in patients suspected of having this deficiency. The absence of unusual bacterial or fungal infections points to a defect in a viral sensor rather than an external TLR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NOD2 alterations are associated with chronic inflammatory disorders such as Crohn disease and sarcoidosis, not severe herpesvirus infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TLR4 recognizes bacterial LPS; its deficiency would not selectively predispose to herpesvirus infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TLR5 recognizes flagellin from bacteria, not a viral PAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD16 is the NK-cell antibody receptor for ADCC, not a pattern recognition receptor.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer develops a dangerously low neutrophil count. She is given a recombinant cytokine that stimulates the bone marrow to produce white blood cells. Which of the following is the most likely cytokine?

explanation.summary: Granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) is a cytokine with a role in normal cell function: it stimulates the bone marrow to make white blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that some cytokines have a role in normal cell function and gives G-CSF as the example, stating that it stimulates the bone marrow to make white blood cells. Its review section adds that G-CSF is a white blood cell growth factor that stimulates stem cells to produce granulocytes and monocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IFN-gamma activates macrophages and increases MHC expression rather than driving marrow production of leukocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits immune cell activation; it does not stimulate white blood cell production.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-8 is a chemokine that recruits neutrophils from the blood into inflamed tissue; it does not stimulate their production in the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta suppresses most innate and adaptive immune cells and promotes wound healing.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with community-acquired bacterial pneumonia has a temperature of 39.0 C and reports loss of appetite. Laboratory studies show a marked rise in acute phase reactant proteins. Although several pro-inflammatory cytokines contribute, which of the following is the most important inducer of these acute phase reactants?

explanation.summary: IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha all induce acute phase reactants, but IL-6 does so most prominently.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that IL-6, IL-1, and TNF-alpha are the three major pro-inflammatory cytokines and that all three, but particularly IL-6, induce acute phase reactants, proteins or polypeptides that increase or decrease in response to inflammation. The brick's table lists IL-6 as inducing fever and the acute phase reaction and being released by activated immune cells and stromal cells. All three also decrease appetite and act as pyrogens, matching this patient's fever and anorexia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-alpha is a type I interferon with antiviral function, not an inducer of the acute phase reaction.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory and inhibits the action of the pro-inflammatory cytokines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-12 is produced by activated macrophages and activates NK cells; it is not the cytokine the brick links to acute phase reactants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-8 is a chemokine that recruits neutrophils; it is not described as an inducer of acute phase reactants.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl with acute bacterial otitis media has a temperature of 39.4 C and refuses to eat. Her fever results from a pro-inflammatory cytokine that resets the thermostat of the central nervous system in the hypothalamus. Which of the following cytokines is most likely responsible?

explanation.summary: IL-1 is a pyrogen that produces fever by resetting the hypothalamic thermostat.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes IL-1 as a major pro-inflammatory cytokine that acts as a pyrogen, a substance that produces fever, and that can decrease appetite. Its review section explains that IL-1 causes fever by resetting the central nervous system thermostat in the hypothalamus and notes that the high temperature helps inhibit bacterial and viral growth. IL-6 and TNF-alpha also cause fever.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory and inhibits the inflammatory response to TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-2 is produced by T cells to increase T-cell proliferation and activate B cells; it is not a pyrogen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 is produced by T cells and signals immunoglobulin switching; it decreases production of pro-inflammatory cytokines rather than causing fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta suppresses most immune cells and promotes wound healing; it does not produce fever.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with Crohn disease is started on infliximab. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug reduces inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fusion protein that serves as a decoy receptor for soluble TNF-alpha

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody that binds soluble TNF-alpha and blocks receptor binding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody that blocks the IL-1 receptor on responding cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monoclonal antibody that neutralizes LPS before it reaches TLR4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small molecule that prevents NF-κB from entering the nucleus

explanation.summary: Infliximab and adalimumab are monoclonal antibodies that bind soluble TNF-alpha and block it from binding its receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, because of its importance in inflammation, monoclonal antibodies that bind soluble TNF-alpha and block receptor binding (adalimumab, infliximab) are used to treat inflammatory conditions. The accompanying figure shows infliximab binding both soluble and membrane forms of TNF-alpha and preventing engagement of the TNF receptor. The brick notes these drugs carry a risk of immunosuppression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A fusion protein acting as a decoy receptor describes etanercept, not infliximab.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infliximab targets TNF-alpha, not the IL-1 receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infliximab neutralizes TNF-alpha, a host cytokine, not the bacterial PAMP LPS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infliximab is an antibody that acts on extracellular TNF-alpha; it does not enter cells to block NF-κB translocation.

questions.stem: In an experiment, mice whose neutrophils lack the IL-8 receptor are injected subcutaneously with bacteria.
