Neutrophil recruitment to the site is reduced but not abolished, because other chemoattractants generated at the site of infection still draw neutrophils from the blood. Which of the following is one such neutrophil chemoattractant?

explanation.summary: IL-8, complement components, and leukotriene B4 (LTB4) are the neutrophil chemoattractants named in the innate response to an extracellular pathogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: In its step-by-step account of leukocyte migration into tissues, the brick states that IL-8, complement components, and leukotriene B4 (LTB4) are neutrophil chemoattractants, while IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha increase adhesion molecules on endothelium. Loss of IL-8 signaling alone therefore reduces but does not eliminate neutrophil recruitment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine, released from mast cell granules, mediates increased vascular permeability and vasodilation rather than neutrophil chemotaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits immune cell activation; it does not attract neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactoferrin is an antimicrobial protein that kills or inhibits microbes; it is not a chemoattractant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins sensitize nerves and cause pain; they are not listed as neutrophil chemoattractants.

questions.stem: Cultured epithelial cells are exposed to IFN-beta. Within hours, ribosomes in the cells fail to initiate translation of both viral and host mRNAs, although the mRNAs themselves remain intact, and subsequent viral replication is markedly impaired. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this effect?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased expression of MHC class I

explanation.summary: Type I interferons induce enzymes that inhibit eIF-2, blocking translation initiation and selectively inhibiting metabolism in infected cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that type I interferons induce transcription of antiviral enzymes. RNase L degrades RNA in the presence of virus-specific double-stranded RNA, and other enzymes inhibit eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF-2), blocking translation initiation. Together these changes selectively inhibit metabolism in infected cells, making it more difficult for the virus to spread. Because the mRNAs here are intact but translation fails to start, the eIF-2 block is the responsible mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RNase L degrades RNA; the intact mRNAs in this experiment argue against RNA degradation as the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granzyme cleavage of caspases is the NK-cell apoptosis mechanism, not an interferon-induced translational block.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NF-κB is a transcription factor in PRR signaling; the brick does not describe type I IFN acting by suppressing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased MHC class I helps cytotoxic T cells find infected cells; it does not block translation.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C virus infection is treated with a recombinant cytokine chosen for its potent antiviral properties. Which of the following cytokines is most likely being administered?

explanation.summary: Type I interferons (IFN-alpha and IFN-beta) are used to treat chronic hepatitis B and C because of their potent antiviral properties.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation states that, because of their potent antiviral properties, type I interferons are used to treat chronic hepatitis B and C viral infections. IFN-alpha is one of the two main type I interferons, which induce antiviral enzymes and increase MHC class I expression in infected and neighboring cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IFN-gamma is the type II interferon that mainly activates macrophages; the brick names type I interferons as the hepatitis therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-1 is a pro-inflammatory pyrogen and is not used as an antiviral therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 suppresses immune activation and would not be used to control a chronic viral infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine; high levels induce shock, and it is a drug target rather than a therapy.

questions.stem: During an acute viral infection, activated macrophages in the infected tissue secrete a cytokine that further activates NK cells, enhancing their ability to kill infected cells. Which of the following is this macrophage-derived cytokine?

explanation.summary: IL-12 secreted by activated macrophages, like type I interferons secreted by infected cells, further activates NK cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that type I interferons, secreted by infected cells, or IL-12, secreted by activated macrophages, further activate NK cells. Stimulatory cytokines are one of the three factors promoting NK-cell activation in the brick's figure, along with decreased MHC class I and increased activating ligand signals. The brick also lists IL-12 among the cytokines produced by activated macrophages.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-10 inhibits innate and adaptive immune cell activation rather than stimulating NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-6 is a pyrogen and inducer of acute phase reactants; the brick does not describe it as an NK-cell activator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-8 is a macrophage-derived chemokine, but its role is to recruit neutrophils, not to activate NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta suppresses most immune cells and would dampen rather than enhance NK activity.

questions.stem: A researcher isolates a cytokine that is released by virtually all leukocytes. When added to cultures, it inhibits the activity of T cells, B cells, macrophages, and granulocytes and promotes wound healing. Which of the following is this cytokine?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta is an anti-inflammatory cytokine released by virtually all leukocytes that suppresses most innate and adaptive immune cells and promotes wound healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that TGF-beta suppresses the activity of most immune cells in the innate and adaptive systems, including T and B cells, macrophages, and granulocytes. Its cytokine table lists TGF-beta as inhibiting most innate and adaptive immune cells and promoting wound healing, released by virtually all leukocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma activates macrophages and enhances cytotoxic T and NK cells rather than suppressing them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is produced by macrophages, dendritic cells, and regulatory T cells, not virtually all leukocytes, and the table does not attribute wound healing to it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-12 is produced by activated macrophages to activate NK cells; it is not immunosuppressive.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-6 is pro-inflammatory, inducing fever and the acute phase reaction.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man sustains a contaminated laceration. Four days later the bacteria have been cleared and the wound is beginning to heal. Which of the following cellular events is most directly responsible for resolving the inflammatory response at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activated macrophages secreting IL-8 to recruit neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dendritic cells migrating to secondary lymphoid organs

choices.label: C
choices.text: IFN-gamma-activated macrophages secreting IL-1 and TNF-alpha

choices.label: D
choices.text: M2 macrophages secreting IL-10 and TGF-beta

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mast cells releasing histamine and tryptase

explanation.summary: After microbes are cleared, M2 macrophages secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta to resolve the immune response and promote wound healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The final step of the brick's innate response to an extracellular pathogen is resolution from macrophages: after clearing of the microbes, specific macrophages called M2 macrophages secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta to resolve the immune response and promote wound healing. These are the anti-inflammatory cytokines that prevent excessive inflammation from damaging tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-8-driven neutrophil recruitment is a step in mounting the inflammatory response, not in ending it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dendritic cells move to secondary lymphoid organs to activate T cells; this initiates adaptive immunity rather than resolving inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IFN-gamma-activated macrophages producing IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-8, and IL-12 drive the early inflammatory phase, not its resolution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mast cell degranulation occurs early, when tissue trauma and complement activate sentinel cells, producing vasodilation and permeability.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman is admitted with acute cholecystitis. Her temperature is 37.6 C, heart rate is 84/min, and respiratory rate is 18/min. Leukocyte count is 10,500/mm3 with 4% bands. Arterial blood gas shows a PaCO2 of 29 mm Hg. Which of the following findings satisfies a diagnostic criterion for systemic inflammatory response syndrome in this patient?

explanation.summary: The respiratory SIRS criterion is met by either a respiratory rate above 20 or a PaCO2 below 32 mm Hg.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's figure lists the SIRS criteria as temperature above 38 C or below 36 C, heart rate above 90, respiratory rate above 20 or PaCO2 below 32, and white blood cells above 12,000 or below 4,000 or more than 10% bands. A PaCO2 of 29 mm Hg is below 32 and therefore satisfies the respiratory criterion even though her respiratory rate is only 18. She meets only one criterion, so she does not yet have SIRS, which requires at least two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bands of 4% do not exceed the 10% threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A heart rate of 84/min does not exceed the threshold of 90.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A leukocyte count of 10,500/mm3 is between 4,000 and 12,000 and does not meet the white blood cell criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A temperature of 37.6 C is within the 36 to 38 C range and does not meet the temperature criterion.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis has a temperature of 38.6 C, heart rate of 118/min, respiratory rate of 26/min, and leukocyte count of 17,000/mm3. Blood, urine, and peritoneal fluid cultures are all negative, and no infectious source is identified. Which of the following best classifies his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Localized inflammation confined to the pancreas

explanation.summary: Non-infectious severe stressors such as pancreatitis or multisystem trauma can trigger SIRS; without infection the condition is SIRS, not sepsis.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient meets all four SIRS criteria (temperature above 38 C, heart rate above 90, respiratory rate above 20, and leukocytes above 12,000). The brick emphasizes that although infection-associated PAMPs and DAMPs are one cause of SIRS, non-infectious severe stressors such as pancreatitis or multisystem trauma can also trigger it. Its clinical correlation notes that over 30% of inpatients and over 50% of ICU patients meet SIRS criteria, including those admitted for non-infectious causes such as myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, and substance abuse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: His systemic vital sign and leukocyte abnormalities show that the inflammatory response is systemic, not confined to the pancreas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MODS is septic shock plus multiple organ system damage; there is no organ failure described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sepsis is SIRS in the presence of infection; his cultures are negative and no infectious source has been found.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Septic shock requires sepsis plus persistent hypotension despite IV fluids, neither of which is present.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with Escherichia coli urinary tract infection and bacteremia has a blood pressure of 76/40 mm Hg that fails to improve after several liters of IV fluids. Which of the following best explains his persistent hypotension?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokine-induced systemic vasodilation and capillary leakage

choices.label: B
choices.text: Granzyme-mediated cleavage of caspases in cardiac myocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL-10-mediated suppression of adhesion molecule expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: NK cell-mediated apoptosis of vascular endothelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type I interferon-mediated inhibition of cellular metabolism

explanation.summary: Septic shock occurs when cytokine-induced systemic vasodilation produces persistent hypotension despite IV fluids; this reflects a cytokine storm driven by LPS and TLR4.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that high levels of LPS and extensive activation of TLR4 can produce a dysregulated response in which a positive feedback loop of inflammation, a cytokine storm, causes systemic dysregulation including vasodilation and capillary leakage. Septic shock is defined as sepsis with hypotension despite IV fluids, occurring when cytokine-induced systemic vasodilation results in persistent hypotension. Mortality rises at each step, exceeding 50% once multi-organ dysfunction syndrome develops.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granzymes act on NK-cell targets to induce apoptosis; they are not the cause of vasodilation in sepsis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 is anti-inflammatory; its action would dampen rather than produce the dysregulated vasodilation of shock.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK cells kill virus-infected or MHC-I-low cells; endothelial apoptosis by NK cells is not the mechanism of septic hypotension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type I interferon-induced metabolic inhibition is an antiviral mechanism within infected cells and does not cause systemic hypotension.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman scrapes her forearm. Within minutes the area becomes red and swollen. A granulocyte residing just below the capillaries has been activated directly by the tissue trauma and by complement, releasing histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes, and tryptase from its granules. Which of the following is this cell?

explanation.summary: Mast cells are sentinel granulocytes below the capillaries that degranulate in response to trauma and complement, releasing histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes, and tryptase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick names three sentinel cell types: macrophages, dendritic cells, and mast cells. Mast cells are granulocytes that reside just below the capillaries and can be activated by tissue trauma and complement. Activated mast cells release histamine, bradykinin, leukotrienes, and tryptase from their granules; histamine and bradykinin, with TNF-alpha, mediate the vascular permeability and vasodilation that produce swelling and redness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells that migrate to secondary lymphoid organs to activate T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages are phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells that secrete cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha; they are not granulocytes releasing histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK cells are lymphocytes that induce apoptosis in virus-infected cells and are not granulocytes below the capillaries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are recruited from the blood over hours as first responders; they are not the resident cell releasing histamine within minutes.

questions.stem: Two patients each sustain a small cut on the hand. In the first, the wound becomes infected with bacteria; in the second, the wound introduces only a virus. Both wounds become red and swollen, but the bacterial wound develops abundant pus while the viral wound develops very little. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PRRs sensing viral PAMPs induce type I interferons rather than neutrophil chemokines

choices.label: B
choices.text: Type I interferons directly kill neutrophils that reach the infected site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Viral PAMPs bind NOD-like receptors, which suppress inflammasome formation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Virus-infected cells downregulate MHC class I, preventing neutrophil recognition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viruses do not damage tissue, so no DAMPs are released to activate sentinel cells

explanation.summary: Viral PAMPs drive type I interferon production, which protects neighboring cells but is not a neutrophil chemokine, so less neutrophil recruitment and less pus occur.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's case conclusion explains that if the cut had introduced only a viral infection, less pus would be expected because of reduced neutrophil recruitment. The PRRs that sense viral PAMPs in infected cells induce different cytokines, specifically type I interferons, which protect neighboring cells but are not neutrophil chemokines. NK cells would instead be activated to induce apoptosis of infected cells. In the bacterial wound, neutrophil activation is what induces the formation of pus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Type I interferons induce antiviral enzymes in neighboring cells; they are not described as killing neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick does not describe viral PAMPs suppressing inflammasomes; NLRs form inflammasomes that produce IL-1.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I downregulation is a viral evasion of cytotoxic T cells that NK cells detect; it has nothing to do with neutrophil recruitment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Virus-infected cells express DAMPs if significantly damaged, and the brick describes viral PAMPs and tissue DAMPs activating sentinel cells.

questions.stem: A tumor cell line expresses normal levels of MHC class I but has high surface expression of stress-induced ligands. When co-cultured with NK cells, the tumor cells are efficiently killed. Which of the following best explains the NK-cell activation in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgG bound to the tumor surface engages CD16 on the NK cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of the inhibitory MHC class I signal releases the NK cell from inhibition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stress ligands are presented as peptides to the antigen receptor of the NK cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stress ligands engage NK activating receptors and override MHC class I inhibition

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor-secreted IL-12 provides a stimulatory cytokine signal to the NK cell

explanation.summary: An increased activating ligand signal is one of the three factors that promote NK-cell activation, alongside stimulatory cytokines and decreased MHC class I.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's NK-activation figure lists three factors that promote NK-cell activation: stimulatory cytokines, a decreased MHC class I signal, and an increased activating ligand signal. It shows a stimulatory ligand on the target engaging an activating receptor on the NK cell, and summarizes that NK cells recognize cells that lack MHC or express stress ligands. Here MHC class I is normal, so the stress ligand-activating receptor signal is what triggers lytic granule release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antibody is present in this co-culture, so CD16-mediated ADCC cannot explain the killing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MHC class I expression is normal on these tumor cells, so the missing-self mechanism does not apply.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NK cells are lymphocytes that do not express antigen receptors, so they cannot recognize presented peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-12 is secreted by activated macrophages, not tumor cells, and no macrophages are present.

questions.stem: NK cells from a patient with an inherited perforin deficiency are co-cultured with virus-infected target cells. Although granule-mediated killing is absent, a subset of targets still undergoes caspase-dependent apoptosis after NK-cell contact. Which of the following best explains this residual killing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Defensins released from NK granules lyse the target membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: FasL on the NK cell binds Fas on the target cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granzymes enter the target through pores formed by lysozyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG secreted by the NK cell opsonizes the target for complement lysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type I interferon from the NK cell activates RNase L in the target

explanation.summary: NK cells induce apoptosis in two ways: perforin/granzyme granules and FasL binding to Fas, which triggers caspase signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that NK cells can induce apoptosis in target cells in two ways. First, they release cytolytic granules containing perforin and granzymes. Second, NK cells express FasL, which binds Fas on the target and induces caspase signaling and apoptosis. Without perforin, granzymes cannot enter the target, so the Fas pathway accounts for the remaining caspase-dependent killing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defensins are antimicrobial peptides that kill or inhibit microbes; they are not the NK mechanism for inducing target-cell apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysozyme is an antimicrobial enzyme that degrades microbes; it does not form pores for granzyme entry, and perforin is the pore-former.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK cells do not secrete antibodies; in ADCC they bind IgG made by other cells via CD16.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type I interferons are produced by virus-infected cells, not NK cells, and they induce an antiviral state rather than caspase-dependent apoptosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with COVID-19 develops acute respiratory distress with markedly elevated serum TNF-alpha and IL-6 and sustained NF-κB activation in lung tissue. Compared with patients who had mild disease, which of the following was most likely present in this patient early in the infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of TLR4 on alveolar macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive production of IL-10 by regulatory T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased perforin release by NK cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of MHC class I expression on infected lung cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced production and activity of type I interferon

explanation.summary: In the most severe forms of COVID-19, type I interferon production and activity are strongly reduced, leading to poor viral control, sustained PRR and NF-κB activation, and excess TNF-alpha and IL-6.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical correlation notes that the production and activity of type I IFN are strongly reduced in the most severe forms of COVID-19. The resulting poor control of the infection causes sustained activation of PRRs, NF-κB activation, and increased production of TNF-alpha and IL-6. The increased inflammation in the lungs can harm the tissue and cause acute respiratory distress.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of TLR4 would reduce, not sustain, PRR signaling, and TLR4 senses bacterial LPS rather than a viral PAMP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess IL-10 would suppress inflammation, which is the opposite of the sustained inflammatory activation seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased NK killing would improve viral control; the brick attributes severe disease to a deficient, not an excessive, antiviral response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I downregulation is a viral evasion of cytotoxic T cells recognized by NK cells; it is not the mechanism the brick links to severe COVID-19.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted with lobar pneumonia. Her leukocyte count is markedly elevated with a left shift. A peripheral blood smear shows a predominance of cells with a multilobed, segmented nucleus and pale granules, and these cells are the first to enter the infected lung tissue. Which cell type is being described?

explanation.summary: Neutrophils are the most numerous leukocytes and the first phagocytes to enter infected tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils make up 40-70% of blood leukocytes and are the first cells to migrate from the bloodstream into tissue, peaking 2-6 hours after infection. Mature neutrophils are polymorphonuclear cells with a multilobed, segmented nucleus, which matches the smear. A rising count with a left shift (band forms) is typical of a bacterial infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dendritic cells are star-shaped antigen-presenting cells that migrate to lymph nodes, not the dominant blood cell in this smear.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Monocytes have a large horseshoe- or kidney-shaped nucleus, not a multilobed one, and make up only 2-8% of leukocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NK cells target virus-infected cells; viral infections raise lymphocytes, whereas this bacterial pneumonia raises phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrophages are tissue-resident sentinels with a small round nucleus; they do not arrive first from the blood.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has a history of recurrent abscesses and pneumonias caused by catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. Testing shows his phagocytes ingest bacteria normally but fail to generate a respiratory (oxidative) burst. A defect in which enzyme most likely explains his condition?

explanation.summary: Chronic granulomatous disease results from a NADPH oxidase deficiency that blocks the respiratory burst.
explanation.whyCorrect: NADPH oxidase (phagocyte oxidase) generates superoxide, the first and required step of the oxygen-dependent respiratory burst. A deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease, so phagocytes cannot make ROS. Catalase-positive organisms like S. aureus degrade the small amount of hydrogen peroxide the cells could otherwise borrow, making these patients especially vulnerable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: iNOS produces reactive nitrogen species, a separate killing pathway from the oxidative burst described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysozyme degrades peptidoglycan and is not part of the oxygen-dependent burst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid downstream; its deficiency is usually mild, and the burst would still start.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide dismutase acts after superoxide is already made; loss of it would not abolish the initial burst as described.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with pneumococcal sepsis has a very high serum level of an acute phase protein made by the liver. This protein binds the surface of the bacteria and coats them so that neutrophils and macrophages can ingest them more efficiently. Which protein is acting in this way?

explanation.summary: C-reactive protein is a liver-derived acute phase protein that acts as an opsonin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opsonins coat the surface of a pathogen and make phagocytosis faster and more efficient. The brick lists C-reactive protein, along with the complement proteins C3b/C5b and antibodies IgG/IgM, as opsonins recognized by phagocytes. CRP is produced by the liver in response to IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, so it rises steeply in bacterial infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Defensins form pores in microbial membranes rather than tagging pathogens for phagocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine is a vasoactive mediator of inflammation, not a liver-derived opsonin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactoferrin starves bacteria of iron; it is not an opsonin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysozyme degrades bacterial peptidoglycan inside the phagolysosome; it does not opsonize pathogens for uptake.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman develops a fever of 39.2 C during a bacterial infection. Proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1-beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha) have leaked into her blood. Which mediator most directly acts on the hypothalamus to raise the body temperature set point?

explanation.summary: Proinflammatory cytokines induce prostaglandins, which act on the hypothalamus to produce fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-1-beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha induce production of prostaglandins, lipid compounds derived from arachidonic acid and made by almost all cells. Receptors for prostaglandins in the hypothalamus then raise the body temperature set point, producing fever. The cytokines are upstream inducers, but the prostaglandins are the mediators acting directly on the hypothalamus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GM-CSF stimulates the bone marrow to make more granulocytes and monocytes; it does not cause fever directly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-8 (CXCL8) is a chemokine that recruits neutrophils to sites of inflammation, not a hypothalamic pyrogen mediator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactoferrin sequesters iron inside phagolysosomes and has no role in setting body temperature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nitric oxide is a reactive nitrogen species used to kill microbes, not the fever mediator acting on the hypothalamus.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis is being treated. His response to the intracellular pathogen depends on a cytokine that activates macrophages down the M1 pathway, enhancing phagolysosome fusion and the oxidative burst so hidden bacteria can be killed. Which cytokine is chiefly responsible?

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma drives M1 macrophage activation, which is critical for killing intracellular pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: M1 macrophages are activated by PRR ligands or by IFN-gamma and excel at phagocytosis and production of ROS and NO. IFN-gamma is critical for protection against intracellular pathogens because it enhances phagosome-lysosome fusion and the oxidative burst, helping macrophages kill organisms such as the tuberculosis bacterium that otherwise hide inside them.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that suppresses macrophage activation, the opposite of what is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-13, like IL-4, drives the M2 repair phenotype rather than M1 microbial killing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 promotes the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype, which favors repair rather than intracellular killing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta induces M2 polarization and suppresses proinflammatory function.

questions.stem: An immunology student is asked which cell in a peripheral tissue is best equipped to activate naive CD4+ helper T cells. The correct cell expresses high levels of MHC class II in addition to MHC class I. Which cell should the student choose?

explanation.summary: Professional antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells express MHC II to activate helper T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: All nucleated cells express MHC I, which activates cytotoxic T cells, but only professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells) express high levels of MHC II. MHC II is required to activate CD4+ helper T cells, so among the options the dendritic cell is the professional APC.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T cells are activated by MHC I; they are not antigen-presenting cells for helper T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythrocytes lack a nucleus and do not express MHC molecules at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils are phagocytes but are not professional antigen-presenting cells and do not present via high MHC II.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets are anucleate cell fragments and cannot present antigen on MHC II.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man has a skin infection on his forearm. A phagocyte at the site captures antigen, then leaves the tissue, travels to the draining lymph node, and presents the antigen to T cells there. Which cell characteristically performs this scout-and-messenger role?

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells migrate from infected tissue to lymph nodes to present antigen to T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: While macrophages stay in the tissue to fight, dendritic cells leave at the first sign of danger and migrate to local lymph nodes to show antigen to T cells. On activation they upregulate the chemokine receptor CCR7, which recognizes CCL19 and CCL21 and draws them out of tissue toward the lymph node. This delivers antigen to naive T cells to start the adaptive response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Monocytes circulate in the blood and differentiate into macrophages or DCs on entering tissue; they are not the migrating presenter here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NK cells kill virus-infected cells and are not antigen-presenting migratory cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils act locally at the site of inflammation and do not carry antigen to lymph nodes to prime T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tissue-resident macrophages remain at the site of infection rather than migrating to the lymph node.

questions.stem: A patient with a severe bacterial abscess produces thick green pus. In the lab, neutrophils at the site are seen expelling sticky, web-like strands of their own DNA studded with antimicrobial granule contents that trap and immobilize bacteria. Which neutrophil process is depicted?

explanation.summary: NETosis is a last-ditch neutrophil process that expels DNA nets to trap pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: In NETosis, a neutrophil uncoils its DNA into a web-like structure, opens its granules, and explodes, sending the sticky DNA net out of the cell to trap pathogens and stop them from moving. The attached granule contents, including the green enzyme myeloperoxidase, help explain why pus is green. This process is highly inflammatory and recruits more neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen presentation is display of peptide on MHC; it is not the DNA-net trapping described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Classical apoptosis is a quiet, non-inflammatory cell death that does not eject DNA to trap microbes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen by molecules like C3b or antibody, not the release of DNA nets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phagolysosome fusion is intracellular killing after ingestion, not the extracellular DNA trap shown here.

questions.stem: On a peripheral blood smear, a leukocyte is larger than a neutrophil, makes up roughly 2-8% of white cells, and has a large, lightly staining, horseshoe-shaped nucleus. This circulating cell can leave the blood and differentiate into either a tissue macrophage or a dendritic cell. Which cell is it?

explanation.summary: Monocytes are circulating phagocytes with a horseshoe nucleus that become macrophages or DCs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monocytes make up 2-8% of blood leukocytes, are larger than neutrophils, and have a large, horseshoe-shaped nucleus. They circulate in the blood and, when recruited into tissue, differentiate into tissue macrophages or dendritic cells, replenishing those populations during an immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dendritic cells are star-shaped tissue cells with dendrite-like projections, not circulating horseshoe-nucleus cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocytes are small cells with a large round nucleus and thin cytoplasm, and they are not phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages are the tissue-resident product of monocytes, not the circulating blood cell described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils have a multilobed segmented nucleus and are the most numerous leukocyte, not the 2-8% horseshoe-nucleus cell.

questions.stem: Five days after a laceration, the macrophages at the injury site have shifted to an anti-inflammatory phenotype induced by TGF-beta and IL-4. They now secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta and stop the M1 program. What is the primary role of these macrophages at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expel DNA nets to trap remaining bacteria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generate reactive oxygen species to kill microbes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induce fever by acting on the hypothalamus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Present antigen to cytotoxic T cells for viral clearance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Promote fibroblast proliferation and wound healing

explanation.summary: M2 macrophages are anti-inflammatory cells that drive tissue repair and wound healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: M2 macrophages are induced by TGF-beta, IL-4, IL-10, and IL-13 and are essential for wound healing and tissue repair. They secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta, block proinflammatory cytokines, suppress MHC II and costimulation, and promote fibroblast proliferation. This M2 program begins once an infection clears, turning inflammation into repair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NETosis is a neutrophil process, not a function of anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Generating ROS to kill microbes is an M1 function; the M2 phenotype suppresses that program.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fever is driven by proinflammatory cytokines and prostaglandins, opposite to the anti-inflammatory M2 role.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cross-presenting to cytotoxic T cells is not the defining repair role of M2 macrophages described here.

questions.stem: In a phagolysosome, a macrophage produces a highly reactive, toxic radical using an enzyme that converts the amino acid arginine into citrulline. This radical can combine with superoxide to form peroxynitrite. Which enzyme is responsible for generating this reactive nitrogen species?

explanation.summary: iNOS converts arginine to citrulline and produces nitric oxide, a reactive nitrogen species.
explanation.whyCorrect: To produce reactive nitrogen species, an enzyme called inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) converts the amino acid arginine into citrulline, generating nitric oxide (NO). NO has potent antimicrobial properties and can combine with superoxide to form peroxynitrite, which is toxic to microbes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysozyme degrades peptidoglycan and has no role in making nitric oxide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid, part of the ROS pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH oxidase generates superoxide for reactive oxygen species, not nitric oxide from arginine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide within the ROS pathway.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman develops bacteremia. Antigen from the bloodstream must be delivered to a secondary lymphoid organ so that circulating T and B cells can be screened for a matching receptor. Which organ specializes in filtering blood-borne antigens for this purpose?

explanation.summary: The spleen is the secondary lymphoid organ that filters antigens from the blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antigens enter secondary lymphoid organs in different ways: the spleen filters antigens from the blood, while lymph nodes collect antigens arriving from peripheral tissues via the lymphatics. Because this patient has blood-borne antigen from bacteremia, the spleen is the organ that traps and presents it so circulating lymphocytes can be screened.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bone marrow is a primary lymphoid organ for hematopoiesis and B-cell development, not an antigen filter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymph nodes filter antigens carried in from tissues by the lymphatics, not directly from the blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MALT samples antigens at mucosal surfaces, not blood-borne antigens from the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ where T cells mature; it does not filter antigen for immune responses.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has a wound infection with a gram-positive organism whose cell wall is composed largely of peptidoglycan. Neutrophils ingest the bacteria and fuse lysosomes with the phagosome. Which antimicrobial protein in the phagolysosome directly breaks down this cell wall component?

explanation.summary: Lysozyme degrades peptidoglycan, a major component of most bacterial cell walls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antimicrobial proteins are one of the three main killing mechanisms inside the phagolysosome. Among the antimicrobial compounds found in lysosomes, lysozyme is the one that breaks down peptidoglycan, an important structural component of most bacteria. Losing the wall exposes the bacterium to the other phagolysosomal contents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defensins punch pores in bacterial cell walls rather than enzymatically breaking down peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lactoferrin sequesters iron to starve bacteria; it does not cleave peptidoglycan.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid in the oxidative burst, not an enzyme that digests the cell wall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin is a liver-derived acute phase protein that binds iron; it is not a lysosomal wall-degrading enzyme.

questions.stem: Within a neutrophil phagolysosome, a class of small antimicrobial compounds with broad functions acts most notably by generating pores in bacterial cell walls, causing the bacteria to lose their integrity. Which compound class is described?

explanation.summary: Defensins are lysosomal antimicrobial compounds whose most notable action is pore formation in bacterial cell walls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lysosomes contain several antimicrobial compounds, including lysozyme, defensins, and lactoferrin. Defensins are a class of antimicrobial compounds with broad functions, but their most notable action is to generate pores in bacterial cell walls, which destroys the microbe.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ferritin is an iron-binding acute phase protein made by the liver, not a lysosomal pore-forming compound.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lactoferrin acts by sequestering iron, a critical factor for bacterial growth, rather than by making pores.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lysozyme enzymatically breaks down peptidoglycan; it does not form membrane pores.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proteases are lytic enzymes that break down compounds within the phagolysosome; they are not pore-forming.

questions.stem: Four hours after bacteria enter a skin wound, the first neutrophils to arrive begin releasing a chemokine that specifically calls additional neutrophils from the blood into the inflamed tissue. Which molecule is this?

explanation.summary: IL-8 (CXCL8) is the neutrophil chemokine that neutrophils themselves produce to recruit more neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils produce chemokines to call other cells to sites of inflammation. IL-8, also called CXCL8, is a chemokine for neutrophils, and neutrophils release it themselves, amplifying neutrophil recruitment early in infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GM-CSF stimulates bone marrow production of granulocytes and monocytes; it is a growth factor, not a chemokine that directs cell migration into tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 suppresses chemokine production and proinflammatory cytokines; it does not attract neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-12 is made by M1 macrophages to activate NK cells and cytotoxic T cells; it is not a neutrophil chemoattractant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is an anti-inflammatory M2 cytokine that suppresses immune cells and promotes fibroblast proliferation.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy from a 50-year-old man shows tissue-resident phagocytes lining the hepatic sinusoids. These cells are macrophages that carry a tissue-specific name. What are they called?

explanation.summary: Macrophages in the liver are called Kupffer cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophages have different names and attributes depending on the tissue in which they reside. Macrophages in the liver are called Kupffer cells, whereas macrophages in the brain are called microglial cells. The tissue also shapes their appearance and function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alveolar macrophages reside in the lungs, where they are rounded with small projections and help maintain surfactant levels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Band neutrophils are immature circulating granulocytes, not tissue-resident macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Langerhans cells are the dendritic cells of the skin that capture antigen and migrate to lymph nodes, not liver macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Microglial cells are the macrophages of the brain, with long branching processes and a small cell body.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has had 5 days of fever, fatigue, and sore throat. A peripheral blood smear shows a marked increase in small cells with a large round nucleus and thin rim of cytoplasm, while the number of multilobed granular cells is normal. Which category of infection is most consistent with this smear?

explanation.summary: Viral infections raise lymphocytes, whereas bacterial and fungal infections raise phagocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the innate response, bacterial and fungal infections are cleared by phagocytes, while viruses are killed by NK cells. A hematologist can often tell from a smear what kind of infection a patient has: a bacterial infection increases phagocytes such as neutrophils, while viral infections cause an increase in lymphocytes. The elevated lymphocytes with normal neutrophils here point to a viral infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bacterial infection would raise phagocytes, especially neutrophils, rather than lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic granulomatous disease is a NADPH oxidase defect that causes recurrent bacterial infections; it is not what a lymphocyte-predominant smear indicates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fungal infections, like bacterial ones, are cleared by phagocytes and would increase those cells rather than lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperglycemia suppresses phagocyte function; it does not produce a lymphocytosis.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with pyelonephritis has a leukocyte count of 19,000/mm3. Her smear shows many neutrophils with a curved, unsegmented C-shaped nucleus that are normally rare in the blood. As these cells mature over the next days, which change in their nucleus is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It becomes divided into multiple segmented lobes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It becomes horseshoe-shaped and shifts off-center

choices.label: C
choices.text: It becomes large and round with a thin cytoplasmic rim

choices.label: D
choices.text: It becomes small and round with long branching processes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uncoils into a web-like extracellular structure

explanation.summary: Band neutrophils are immature forms whose nuclei become more segmented as they mature into segs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both mature and immature neutrophils can appear on a blood preparation. Immature neutrophils are rarely present in blood but increase during some infections. As neutrophils mature their nuclei become more segmented, so immature and mature forms are called band and segmented neutrophils, respectively. Bands have a C-shaped nucleus that will develop into the multilobed nucleus of a mature PMN.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A large horseshoe-shaped, off-centered nucleus is the hallmark of a monocyte, not a maturing neutrophil.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A large round nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm describes a lymphocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A small cell body with long branching processes describes resting microglia, a tissue macrophage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncoiling DNA into an extracellular web is NETosis, a death process, not a step in neutrophil maturation.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a large abscess in which neutrophils are dying in great numbers. Neutrophils at the site release a cytokine that acts on the bone marrow to increase production and differentiation of granulocytes and monocytes, replacing the cells being lost. Which cytokine is this?

explanation.summary: GM-CSF from neutrophils drives the bone marrow to replenish granulocytes and monocytes lost at the site of infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils release granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), a cytokine that promotes the production and differentiation of granulocytes (including neutrophils) and monocytes from the bone marrow. Elevated GM-CSF helps replenish the neutrophils and other white blood cells dying at the site of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IFN-gamma activates M1 macrophages and enhances their killing of intracellular pathogens rather than acting on the marrow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-12 is produced by M1 macrophages to activate NK cells and cytotoxic T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-6 is a proinflammatory cytokine that induces fever and hepatic acute phase proteins; it is not the marrow growth factor described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-8 is a chemokine that draws neutrophils into inflamed tissue; it does not stimulate bone marrow production.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with an inherited complement deficiency has recurrent bacterial infections. His neutrophils ingest antibody-coated bacteria normally, but phagocytosis of bacteria coated only by complement is markedly reduced. Which complement product normally coats the bacterial surface to enhance phagocytosis?

explanation.summary: C3b and iC3b are the complement opsonins that coat pathogens for phagocyte receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Opsonins coat the surface of a pathogen and make phagocytosis more likely and more efficient once phagocyte membrane receptors recognize them. The critical opsonins are the complement proteins C3b and iC3b, the antibody classes IgG and IgM, and C-reactive protein. Complement proteins are also acute phase proteins that opsonize indirectly following an enzymatic cascade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3a is a small fragment released during complement activation; it is not the surface-bound fragment that phagocyte receptors recognize as an opsonin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C5a is a small released fragment as well, not a pathogen-coating opsonin like C3b or iC3b.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C9 is a terminal complement component and not the fragment that coats bacteria for phagocytic uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgE is not one of the opsonizing antibody classes; the opsonins among antibodies are IgG and IgM, and IgE is not a complement product in any case.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with pulmonary tuberculosis has normal antibody and complement levels, yet the bacteria persist inside his alveolar macrophages. Which mechanism best explains how this organism survives within the phagocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It degrades MHC II to avoid presentation to T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It induces IL-10 to convert the macrophage to an M2 phenotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: It prevents NADPH oxidase from assembling on the membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes catalase that degrades hydrogen peroxide

choices.label: E
choices.text: It secretes proteins that block lysosome fusion with the phagosome

explanation.summary: The tuberculosis bacterium lives in the phagosome and blocks its fusion with lysosomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some pathogens exploit the phagocytosis pathway to hide from the immune system. The bacterium that causes tuberculosis lives inside the phagosome, where antibodies and complement cannot reach it, and it secretes proteins that block the fusion of lysosomes with the phagosome. Without a phagolysosome, the antimicrobial proteins, ROS, and RNS are never delivered to the bacterium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The described evasion is at the level of the phagosome, not degradation of MHC II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M2 polarization is induced by TGF-beta, IL-4, IL-10, and IL-13 as infections clear; it is not the mechanism by which tuberculosis persists inside the phagosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of NADPH oxidase activity is the defect in chronic granulomatous disease, not the survival strategy of the tuberculosis bacterium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Catalase production is the trick of organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus that endangers CGD patients; it is not the mechanism of intracellular hiding described for tuberculosis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with bacterial sepsis has a fall in serum free iron. Proinflammatory cytokines have stimulated her liver to produce acute phase proteins that bind iron and limit pathogen growth. Which pair of proteins is responsible?

explanation.summary: Ferritin and transferrin are liver-derived acute phase proteins that bind iron to limit pathogen growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The liver responds to IL-1-beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha by producing acute phase proteins. C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, ferritin, and transferrin are all produced by the liver as acute phase proteins. Ferritin and transferrin bind iron, limiting pathogen growth, since iron is a critical factor for bacterial growth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen is an acute phase protein essential for clotting and wound repair, and CRP is an opsonin; neither binds iron.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-6 and TNF-alpha are the proinflammatory cytokines that induce acute phase protein production; they are not iron-binding proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactoferrin does sequester iron, but it is a lysosomal antimicrobial protein, and myeloperoxidase is a granule enzyme; neither is a hepatic acute phase protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lysozyme and defensins are lysosomal antimicrobial proteins inside phagocytes, not liver-derived acute phase proteins.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with fever, productive cough, and consolidation on chest radiograph. His C-reactive protein is 165 mg/L (normal 0.5-3 mg/L). Which of the following is most consistent with a CRP elevation of this magnitude?

explanation.summary: Very high CRP (>100 mg/L) occurs with major trauma and acute bacterial infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: CRP is a marker of general inflammation but is highly non-specific, so its magnitude matters. Slight elevations occur with smoking, diabetes, or pregnancy, and moderate elevations are common in autoimmune disease and cancer. Very high levels, above about 100 mg/L when normal is 0.5-3 mg/L, occur with major trauma and acute bacterial infection, which fits this patient's pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Autoimmune disease typically produces moderate CRP elevation, not the very high level seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Smoking causes only a slight elevation of CRP, not a level above 100 mg/L.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pregnancy is associated with only slight CRP elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diabetes produces only slight CRP elevation.

questions.stem: The mother of a 5-year-old boy with an uncomplicated viral illness and a temperature of 38.4 C asks whether the fever must be treated. The physician explains that a moderate fever can be beneficial. Which statement best describes the physiologic basis for that advice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial peptidoglycan is directly denatured above 37 C

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating neutrophils are triggered to undergo NETosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatic C-reactive protein synthesis rises with temperature

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypothalamic prostaglandin production falls with temperature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Immune cells work better and pathogens replicate worse above 37 C

explanation.summary: Moderate fever enhances immune cell function while inhibiting pathogens that replicate best at 37 C.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most pathogens replicate best at normal human body temperature (37 C or 98.6 F), but moderate fevers actually enhance the function of immune cells. By raising body temperature, the hypothalamus is both indirectly and directly inhibiting the pathogen systemically, which is why a moderate fever should not always be treated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peptidoglycan is broken down by lysozyme inside the phagolysosome, not denatured by a moderate fever.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NETosis is a last-ditch neutrophil response to pathogens it cannot otherwise kill; it is not a systemic effect of fever.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CRP production is driven by IL-1-beta, IL-6, and TNF-alpha acting on the liver, not by temperature, and it is not the benefit of fever.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandins acting on the hypothalamus are what raise the temperature set point; fever does not lower them.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman has an infection with an intracellular bacterium. Her M1 macrophages release a cytokine that activates NK cells and cytotoxic T cells; the stimulated NK cells become better killers and secrete IFN-gamma, which in turn boosts the macrophages' ability to destroy the phagocytized bacteria. Which cytokine starts this loop?

explanation.summary: Macrophage IL-12 activates NK cells, whose IFN-gamma further activates macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: M1 macrophages produce IL-12, which activates both NK cells and cytotoxic T cells. When NK cells are stimulated with IL-12 they become better at destroying infected cells and also secrete IFN-gamma. IFN-gamma then greatly enhances the ability of M1 macrophages to destroy phagocytized pathogens, completing a positive loop.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-1-beta is a proinflammatory vasodilator cytokine that induces fever and acute phase proteins; it does not specifically activate NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-6 acts with IL-1-beta and TNF-alpha on the liver and hypothalamus; it is not the NK-activating cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-8 is a chemokine that recruits neutrophils, not an activator of NK cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory M2 cytokine that suppresses proinflammatory function, the opposite of activating NK cells.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is infected with an intestinal parasite. Dendritic cells in the gut wall are activated through their pattern recognition receptors and release cytokines that direct T cells toward the subset best suited to this type of infection. Which cytokines would these dendritic cells be expected to produce?

explanation.summary: In response to a parasite, dendritic cells produce IL-4 and IL-13.
explanation.whyCorrect: What cytokines dendritic cells produce is highly dependent on which PRRs were activated. In response to a classical bacterial infection such as TLR4 binding, DCs make TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma. In response to a parasite, DCs make IL-4 and IL-13. The cytokines DCs produce help direct T cells to the subset best at fighting that type of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-1-beta and IL-6 are proinflammatory cytokines that drive fever and acute phase proteins; they are not the parasite-specific DC signal described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 and TGF-beta are anti-inflammatory cytokines that induce M2 macrophages as infections clear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma are the DC response to a classical bacterial infection, such as TLR4 binding, not to a parasite.
whyWrongByChoice.E: High levels of type I interferons are produced by a DC subset in response to viral infections.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman has an acute viral infection. A specialized subset of dendritic cells is activated at the site of infection and secretes large amounts of a cytokine group particularly suited to the antiviral response. Which cytokines are these dendritic cells known for producing at high levels?

explanation.summary: A subset of dendritic cells produces high levels of type I interferons in response to viral infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Activated dendritic cells secrete proinflammatory cytokines to initiate an immune response, and the cytokines produced depend on which PRRs were engaged. A subset of DCs is known specifically for its ability to produce high levels of type I interferons in response to viral infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GM-CSF and IL-8 are neutrophil products that replenish and recruit granulocytes; they are not the antiviral DC signal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 and TGF-beta are anti-inflammatory cytokines that induce M2 macrophages and suppress immune cells; they are not the DC antiviral signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-4 and IL-13 are what DCs produce in response to a parasite, not a virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma are the DC response to a classical bacterial infection such as TLR4 binding.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronically elevated blood glucose has had three skin and soft tissue infections in the past year. Which of the following best explains his increased susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of NADPH oxidase activity in neutrophils and monocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess IL-10 secretion by M2 macrophages in the skin and soft tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of blood monocytes to differentiate into tissue macrophages in the skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of MHC class II expression on dermal dendritic cells and macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced phagocyte cytokine release, degranulation, phagocytosis, and killing

explanation.summary: Chronic hyperglycemia broadly suppresses phagocyte function.
explanation.whyCorrect: People with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus (hyperglycemia) are at risk for infections because hyperglycemia has been shown to suppress phagocyte function. Phagocytes from patients with chronic hyperglycemia show reduced cytokine production, degranulation, phagocytosis, NET formation, and microbial killing, which impairs the early innate clearance of bacteria in the skin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complete loss of NADPH oxidase is the inherited defect of chronic granulomatous disease, not an acquired effect of hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M2 polarization by IL-10 is the normal repair program after infection clears; it is not the mechanism by which hyperglycemia predisposes to infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation is not the described effect of hyperglycemia; the problem is global suppression of phagocyte effector functions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperglycemia is not described as eliminating MHC II on dendritic cells.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with viral mononucleosis has enlarged, tender lymph nodes in the neck and under the jaw along with an elevated peripheral white blood cell count. Which process best accounts for the enlarged lymph nodes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fibrinogen deposition in the node from the acute phase response

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kupffer cells migrating from the liver into the node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes differentiating into M2 macrophages in the node

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils accumulating and undergoing NETosis in the node

choices.label: E
choices.text: T cells proliferating after activation by migrating dendritic cells

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells carry viral antigen to lymph nodes, where T cells activate and divide, swelling the nodes.
explanation.whyCorrect: In viral mononucleosis, tissue-resident macrophages sense the virus or damaged cells through PRRs and initiate inflammation, and dendritic cells activated at the site of infection migrate to the local lymph nodes to present antigen to T cells. The T cells in the lymph nodes are activated, divide, and are released into the circulation, causing both the increased peripheral white blood cell count and the swollen lymph nodes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrinogen is a hepatic acute phase protein for clotting and wound repair; it does not enlarge lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kupffer cells are tissue-resident liver macrophages and do not migrate to lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M2 differentiation belongs to the repair phase in tissue; it is not the cause of lymphocyte-driven nodal swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils have a smaller role in viral infections, and NETosis is a tissue response to bacteria, not the cause of nodal enlargement here.

questions.stem: A resting naive T cell enters an inguinal lymph node from the blood. During its time in the node it does not encounter any antigen that its T-cell receptor is specific for. What is the expected fate of this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It exits the node and continues circulating through other SLOs

choices.label: B
choices.text: It migrates to the thymus for an additional round of selection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It proliferates in the node regardless of antigen encounter

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stays in the node and differentiates into a memory cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: It undergoes apoptosis and is cleared by node macrophages

explanation.summary: Lymphocytes that do not find cognate antigen in an SLO leave and keep recirculating.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resting T and B cells circulate between secondary lymphoid organs and the vasculature. If a lymphocyte encounters its cognate antigen in an SLO, it stops there, activates, and proliferates, starting the adaptive immune response. If it does not encounter its cognate antigen, it exits back out of the SLO and continues circulating, which maximizes the chance that a lymphocyte and its antigen meet at the right place and time.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The thymus is where T cells mature; circulating naive T cells do not return there when antigen is absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proliferation is triggered only by encounter with cognate antigen in the SLO.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Memory formation requires activation by cognate antigen, which did not occur here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failing to find antigen on one pass does not trigger death; the cell simply moves on to the next SLO.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman is evaluated for a suspected phagocyte defect. Her neutrophils generate normal amounts of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide after ingesting bacteria, but no hypochlorous acid is produced and killing is impaired. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: Myeloperoxidase performs the final step of the oxidative burst, converting hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid.
explanation.whyCorrect: In oxygen-dependent killing, NADPH oxidase first generates superoxide, superoxide dismutase then converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid (HOCl) or hypochlorite, which is potently bactericidal and the most potent product of the burst. Normal superoxide and hydrogen peroxide with absent HOCl localizes the defect to myeloperoxidase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: iNOS makes nitric oxide from arginine, a reactive nitrogen species pathway separate from the HOCl-generating oxidative burst.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysozyme degrades peptidoglycan and plays no role in producing hypochlorous acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH oxidase deficiency (chronic granulomatous disease) abolishes superoxide production, so no portion of the burst would be generated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide dismutase deficiency would block conversion of superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, but hydrogen peroxide is normal here.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with chronic granulomatous disease develops an infection with a catalase-negative bacterium. Despite his enzyme defect, his neutrophils are able to kill this organism. Which of the following best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Intact lactoferrin converts residual hydrogen peroxide to peroxynitrite

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intact lysozyme converts residual hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorite

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intact myeloperoxidase converts residual hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorous acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intact NADPH oxidase converts residual hydrogen peroxide to superoxide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intact superoxide dismutase converts residual hydrogen peroxide to hydroxyl radical

explanation.summary: In CGD the rest of the burst is intact, so hydrogen peroxide from general respiration can still be turned into HOCl unless the microbe destroys it with catalase.
explanation.whyCorrect: A deficiency in NADPH oxidase leads to chronic granulomatous disease, in which phagocytes cannot generate any portion of the respiratory burst themselves. If the rest of the oxidative burst is intact, hydrogen peroxide from general respiration can still be converted by myeloperoxidase to hypochlorous acid. Organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus produce catalase and degrade that hydrogen peroxide, so CGD patients are at high risk from catalase-positive organisms, whereas catalase-negative organisms leave the hydrogen peroxide available for killing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactoferrin sequesters iron and does not act on hydrogen peroxide; peroxynitrite forms from nitric oxide plus superoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysozyme breaks down peptidoglycan and has no role in producing hypochlorite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH oxidase is the deficient enzyme in CGD, and it makes superoxide from oxygen, not from hydrogen peroxide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide dismutase acts upstream, converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide; it does not act on hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem: A researcher compares the antimicrobial products of an IFN-gamma-activated M1 macrophage with those of a neutrophil that ingested the same bacterium. Compared with the neutrophil, the M1 macrophage would be expected to lack significant production of which of the following?

explanation.summary: M1 macrophages are not granulocytes, so they make lysozyme but not significant defensins or lactoferrin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like neutrophils, all macrophages can produce ROS, NO, and cytokines when activated, and M1 macrophages excel at phagocytosis and production of ROS and NO. They make lysozyme, but they are not granulocytes and do not generate significant defensins or lactoferrin, which are granule products characteristic of neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Activated macrophages, especially IFN-gamma-activated ones, are the main producers of IL-1-beta, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IL-8.
whyWrongByChoice.C: M1 macrophages do make lysozyme; it is the granule-associated defensins and lactoferrin they lack.
whyWrongByChoice.D: M1 macrophages produce nitric oxide via iNOS, so NO is not what they lack.
whyWrongByChoice.E: M1 macrophages excel at ROS production through the oxidative burst.

questions.stem: Ten days after a deep laceration, M2 macrophages in the wound are secreting two anti-inflammatory cytokines. One of them suppresses the activity of most immune cells in both the innate and adaptive systems and promotes fibroblast proliferation to rebuild the tissue. Which cytokine has these effects?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta broadly suppresses innate and adaptive immune cells and promotes fibroblast proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike M1 macrophages, M2 macrophages secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta. IL-10 blocks production of proinflammatory cytokines like IL-1 and TNF-alpha, suppresses MHC II and costimulatory molecules, and suppresses chemokine production. TGF-beta, by contrast, suppresses the activity of most immune cells in the innate and adaptive systems and promotes fibroblast proliferation, the effect described here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma drives the proinflammatory M1 program, the opposite of the repair phase described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is the other M2 product, but its described actions are blocking proinflammatory cytokines, MHC II, costimulation, and chemokines, not driving fibroblast proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-13 likewise induces M2 polarization; it is not the M2-secreted cytokine that promotes fibroblast proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 is one of the cytokines that induces the M2 phenotype rather than a fibroblast-stimulating product secreted by M2 cells.

questions.stem: In an experimental mouse strain, lymph nodes fail to express CCL19 and CCL21. After a skin infection, dermal dendritic cells capture antigen, become activated, and upregulate MHC and CCR7 normally, yet very few activated dendritic cells reach the draining lymph node. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Afferent lymphatic vessels draining the skin are absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dendritic cells cannot phagocytose antigen at the infection site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dendritic cells fail to upregulate costimulatory molecules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess IL-10 in the skin suppresses dendritic cell activation

choices.label: E
choices.text: No chemotactic gradient exists to draw CCR7-bearing cells toward the node

explanation.summary: CCR7 on activated DCs follows a CCL19/CCL21 gradient that is highest in secondary lymphoid organs.
explanation.whyCorrect: When DCs are activated they upregulate CCR7, a chemokine receptor that recognizes CCL19 and CCL21. These chemokines are expressed in high concentrations in secondary lymphoid organs like lymph nodes, and the increased CCR7 lets activated DCs follow the CCL19/21 chemotactic gradient out of local tissue toward the lymph nodes. Without CCL19 and CCL21 in the node there is no gradient to follow, so CCR7 expression alone cannot guide migration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The defect described is loss of the chemokines, not of the lymphatic vessels through which DCs travel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem states antigen capture and activation occurred normally; the defect is downstream, in migration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Upregulation of MHC and costimulatory molecules is part of DC activation, which the stem says happened normally, and it does not direct migration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-10 is not part of this scenario, and the DCs were activated normally.

questions.stem: During a skin infection, both free soluble antigen carried in lymph and dendritic cells carrying processed antigen arrive at the draining lymph node. B cells in the node can respond to the free antigen, but naive T cells do not respond to it and instead depend on the dendritic cells. Which of the following best explains why T cells require dendritic cell delivery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B cells sequester free antigen before T cells can bind it

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free antigen cannot pass through afferent lymphatic vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Macrophages lining the node degrade all free antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: T cells leave the node before free antigen arrives

choices.label: E
choices.text: T cells recognize only peptide antigens loaded in MHC

explanation.summary: T cells only recognize peptide in MHC, so DCs must carry antigen to the node in a presentable form.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antigens can enter secondary lymphoid organs in several ways: the spleen filters antigens from blood, and soluble antigens in lymph can move into lymph nodes via the lymphatics. Free antigens are not a problem for B cells, but T cells only recognize peptide antigens in MHC. When activated DCs in peripheral tissues enter lymph vessels and move into lymph nodes, they ensure that antigens arrive at the node in a state that can activate T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells respond to free antigen but do not prevent T cells from encountering it; the limitation is the T-cell receptor's requirement for peptide in MHC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Soluble antigens in lymph do move into lymph nodes via the lymphatics; free antigen reaches the node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages line the lymphatic circulation of the node for non-specific filtering, but that is not why T cells cannot respond to free antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resting T cells circulate through SLOs continuously; timing is not the reason they ignore free antigen.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is referred for recurrent, severe infections with encapsulated bacteria, including Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae, despite having completed all childhood conjugate vaccinations. Laboratory testing shows normal serum C3 and intact opsonization, but the patient's serum is completely unable to lyse antibody-sensitized sheep erythrocytes. Which of the following components is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: A defect in the terminal (shared) pathway prevents membrane attack complex formation, causing recurrent Neisseria infections despite vaccination.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inability to lyse sheep erythrocytes with intact opsonization and normal C3 points to a terminal pathway defect. C5b initiates assembly of the membrane attack complex (C5b-C9); loss of any terminal component (C5-C9) blocks lysis. The brick notes that terminal complement deficiencies cause recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections, especially Neisseria, even in vaccinated patients, and this scenario mirrors the brick's case of a C5-deficient child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1q deficiency impairs the early classical pathway and is associated with lupus-like autoimmunity, not an isolated inability to lyse cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C3 is stated to be normal, and its loss would also cripple opsonization, which is intact here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CR1 is an erythrocyte and phagocyte receptor for C3b involved in immune complex clearance, not in forming the lytic MAC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor D deficiency impairs the alternative pathway convertase, but opsonization and C3 activity would be affected rather than only terminal lysis.

questions.stem: A 16-month-old girl presents with recurrent mouth ulcerations, a malar (butterfly) rash, and elevated liver enzymes suggestive of a lupus-like disorder. Complement testing reveals a markedly reduced CH50 with a normal AH50, and her symptoms improve substantially with regular fresh frozen plasma infusions. A deficiency of which of the following proteins best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: A low CH50 with a normal AH50 localizes the defect to a component unique to the classical pathway (C1, C2, or C4).
explanation.whyCorrect: The CH50 assay measures classical pathway activity while the AH50 measures the alternative pathway. A reduced CH50 with a preserved AH50 indicates a defect in a component used only by the classical pathway, such as C1q, C2, or C4. The brick further links early classical deficiencies (e.g., C1q) to impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic cells, producing lupus-like autoimmunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C9 is a shared terminal component, so its deficiency would lower both the CH50 and the AH50, not just the CH50.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD55 (DAF) is a regulator; its deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not an isolated low CH50.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor B is unique to the alternative pathway, so its loss would reduce the AH50, not selectively lower the CH50.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MBL functions in the lectin pathway, which is not measured by the CH50 assay, so its loss would not selectively drop the CH50.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl has a history of recurrent, painless swelling episodes involving her face, lips, and hands. The swelling is not itchy, lasts 2 to 5 days, occasionally affects the gastrointestinal tract with abdominal pain and vomiting, and on a few occasions has caused difficulty breathing from throat swelling. Antihistamines have not helped. Her mother and grandmother have been diagnosed with the same complement deficiency. Which protein is most likely deficient?

explanation.summary: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, marked by recurrent non-pruritic swelling that does not respond to antihistamines.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lack of C1-INH leads to recurrent complement activation and, importantly, unopposed bradykinin release, a potent vasodilator that produces edema from plasma leakage. The brick describes hereditary angioedema as childhood-onset, non-itchy, antihistamine-resistant swelling that can involve the lips and GI tract and can be life-threatening when the larynx is affected, consistent with this patient's autosomal-dominant family history.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C5 deficiency impairs MAC formation and causes recurrent encapsulated bacterial infections, not angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C9 is a terminal MAC component; its deficiency predisposes to Neisseria infections, not recurrent angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD55 deficiency causes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria with dark urine and hemolysis, not episodic bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor D deficiency impairs the alternative pathway and increases infection risk, not swelling episodes.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with known hereditary angioedema due to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency is started on a new antihypertensive medication.
