Two weeks later he develops a severe attack of facial and laryngeal swelling. Which of the following newly prescribed medications most likely precipitated this attack?

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors block bradykinin degradation and are contraindicated in hereditary angioedema because they worsen bradykinin-mediated swelling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor. The brick states that ACE inhibitors cause bradykinin degradation to be blocked, raising bradykinin levels; because angioedema in C1-INH deficiency is bradykinin-mediated, ACE inhibitors are contraindicated and can even unmask previously hidden HAE. This makes lisinopril the most likely trigger of the attack.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amlodipine is a calcium-channel blocker with no effect on bradykinin degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic and does not affect bradykinin metabolism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Losartan is an angiotensin-receptor blocker that does not inhibit bradykinin breakdown, so it does not carry the same HAE risk as an ACE inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metoprolol is a beta-blocker and does not raise bradykinin levels.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman reports several months of fatigue, intermittent jaundice, and episodes of dark, reddish urine that are most noticeable in the morning. She has also had a deep vein thrombosis. Flow cytometry of her red blood cells shows markedly decreased surface expression of CD55 and CD59. Deficiency of which of the following best explains her hemolysis?

explanation.summary: Loss of the glycolipid anchor for DAF (CD55) and CD59 lets the membrane attack complex form on red cells, causing paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Decay-accelerating factor (CD55) is a membrane-bound protein that blocks C3 convertase formation and is anchored by a glycolipid. When that anchor is defective, both DAF and CD59 are lost, so MACs form on circulating erythrocytes and lyse them. The brick attributes the dark morning urine, hemolysis, fatigue, jaundice, and thrombosis of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria to this loss, diagnosed by low CD55/CD59 on flow cytometry.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1-INH deficiency causes bradykinin-mediated angioedema, not complement-mediated red cell lysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C5 deficiency prevents MAC formation and would protect red cells from lysis rather than cause it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MBL deficiency impairs lectin pathway initiation and does not cause loss of CD55/CD59 or intravascular hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Properdin stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase; its loss predisposes to Neisseria infection, not chronic hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria is started on eculizumab, which markedly reduces his hemolysis. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal antibody that binds C5 and prevents its cleavage

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks C1 esterase activity in the classical pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits Factor D and blocks the alternative convertase

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replaces decay-accelerating factor on the red cell surface

explanation.summary: Eculizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody against C5 that stops formation of C5a and C5b, blocking downstream MAC assembly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients with PNH can be treated with C5 inhibitors like eculizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that inhibits cleavage of C5 into C5a and C5b. Preventing C5b formation blocks the terminal pathway and the membrane attack complex, protecting red cells from complement-mediated lysis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bradykinin receptor antagonism is relevant to angioedema management, not to complement-mediated hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking C1 esterase describes the action of C1-INH, used in hereditary angioedema, not eculizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eculizumab targets C5, not Factor D of the alternative pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eculizumab does not restore or replace the missing DAF/CD59 anchor; it acts upstream by blocking C5.

questions.stem: Which of the following complement components is the most potent anaphylatoxin and most strongly attracts leukocytes to sites of complement activation?

explanation.summary: C5a is the most potent anaphylatoxin and a chemoattractant that recruits and activates leukocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies C5a as the most potent of the inflammatory mediators; it increases vascular permeability and adhesion molecule expression and acts on neutrophils and monocytes to induce phagocytosis and migration. This chemotactic recruitment of leukocytes to sites of complement activation is its defining function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3b is an opsonin recognized by CR1 and a building block of the C5 convertase; it does not recruit leukocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C4b is part of the classical and lectin C3 convertase, not a chemoattractant.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C9 polymerizes to form the membrane attack complex pore and has no chemotactic role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MASPs are serine proteases that cleave C4 and C2 in the lectin pathway, not anaphylatoxins.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man has had two episodes of Neisseria meningitidis meningitis. Complement studies show that he cannot stabilize the alternative pathway C3 convertase, though his classical and lectin pathways function normally. Deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Properdin stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase; its loss predisposes to severe Neisseria infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that properdin stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase (C3bBb), making the complex more resistant to protease degradation. An individual who lacks properdin cannot stabilize this convertase and is highly susceptible to encapsulated bacteria, especially those in the Neisseria genus, matching this patient's recurrent meningococcal disease with an isolated alternative pathway defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1-INH deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, not a failure to stabilize the alternative convertase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C1q initiates the classical pathway, which is stated to be normal in this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CR1 is a receptor for C3b involved in immune complex clearance and opsonin recognition, not convertase stabilization.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD55 (DAF) inhibits convertase formation; its deficiency causes PNH, not decreased convertase stability.

questions.stem: During an antibody-mediated immune response, activation of the classical complement pathway requires binding of C1q to antibody on a pathogen surface. Which of the following antibody isotypes is the most efficient activator of the classical pathway, requiring only a single bound molecule to engage C1q?

explanation.summary: A single pentameric IgM molecule can activate C1q, whereas IgG must have two adjacent molecules bound.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that both IgG and IgM function as opsonins that activate the classical pathway, but because C1q must bind two molecules of monomeric IgG to be activated, whereas IgM is a pentamer, one molecule of IgM is sufficient to activate C1q. This makes IgM the most efficient single-molecule classical pathway activator.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is not described as a classical pathway activator in this context.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD functions mainly as a B cell receptor and is not a classical pathway activator.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE mediates allergic and antiparasitic responses and does not efficiently activate C1q.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG activates the classical pathway only when two adjacent IgG molecules are bound, so a single molecule is not sufficient.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a buildup of circulating immune complexes. In a healthy person, which of the following mechanisms is primarily responsible for clearing such immune complexes from the circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: C1 esterase inhibitor enzymatically degrades the complexes

choices.label: B
choices.text: C3b coats the complexes, which are then bound by CR1 on erythrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: C5a recruits neutrophils that phagocytose the complexes in the bloodstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decay-accelerating factor strips the complexes from cell surfaces

choices.label: E
choices.text: The membrane attack complex directly lyses circulating immune complexes

explanation.summary: C3b-coated immune complexes bind erythrocyte CR1 and are shuttled to the liver and spleen, where phagocytes remove them.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that C3b coats immune complexes and that CR1 on erythrocytes binds this C3b. Red cells carry the complexes to the spleen and liver, where phagocytes such as Kupffer cells strip the complexes off CR1 and destroy them. Reduced CR1 expression, as reported in SLE, impairs this clearance and contributes to immune complex buildup.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1-INH regulates C1 and bradykinin; it does not degrade immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C5a recruits leukocytes to inflamed tissue but is not the primary route for clearing circulating complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DAF is a convertase-blocking regulator on host cells and does not clear immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The MAC lyses cellular membranes, not soluble immune complexes.

questions.stem: All three complement pathways converge on a shared terminal pathway that assembles the membrane attack complex on a target membrane. Which of the following components initiates assembly of the membrane attack complex by binding C6 and C7?

explanation.summary: C5b initiates the terminal pathway by binding C6 and C7, seeding assembly of the membrane attack complex.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that C5b initiates the formation of the MAC; then C6, C7, C8, and multiple copies of C9 bind to complete the complex. Binding of C6 and C7 to C5b exposes a hydrophobic site in C7 that inserts into the membrane, anchoring the growing pore.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1q initiates the classical pathway at the top of the cascade, not terminal MAC assembly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C3b is an opsonin and a component of the C5 convertase, but it does not seed MAC assembly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C4b is part of the classical and lectin C3 convertase, not the terminal complex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C5a is the anaphylatoxin fragment released when C5 is cleaved; it diffuses away and does not join the MAC.

questions.stem: A soluble pattern recognition receptor in the serum binds mannose residues displayed on the surface of an invading bacterium. This binding activates associated serine proteases that then cleave C4 and C2. Which complement activation pathway has been triggered?

explanation.summary: The lectin pathway is initiated by mannose-binding lectin, whose MASPs cleave C4 and C2 to form the C4b2b convertase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the lectin pathway as being initiated by mannose-binding lectin (MBL), a soluble pattern recognition receptor that binds mannose and other sugars in patterns found on pathogens. After MBL binds, MBL-associated serine proteases (MASPs) cleave C2 and C4, generating the same C3 convertase as the classical pathway (C4b2b).

whyWrongByChoice.A: The specific trigger described (MBL binding mannose, MASPs cleaving C4 and C2) is unique to the lectin pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The alternative pathway begins with spontaneous C3 tickover and uses Factors B and D, not MBL and MASPs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The classical pathway is triggered by antibody or CRP binding C1, not by a mannose-binding lectin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The terminal pathway is the shared MAC-forming stage that begins with C5b, downstream of C4 and C2 cleavage.

questions.stem: Complement proteins are ubiquitous, circulating in the blood and interstitial fluid and even reaching the brain, which lets the system act as an early-warning system throughout the body. The more than 40 soluble proteins of the complement system are synthesized predominantly by which of the following?

explanation.summary: Complement proteins are made predominantly by the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the complement system as a group of more than 40 soluble proteins made predominantly by the liver. Because they are secreted into the circulation, they are present in blood, interstitial fluid, and even the brain, allowing complement to function throughout the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow produces blood cells, including the phagocytes that respond to complement, but it is not the main source of complement proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The kidney is not the predominant source of complement proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen filters erythrocytes carrying immune complexes and houses phagocytes, but it is not the predominant site of complement synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymus is a site of T cell development and is not described as a source of complement proteins.

questions.stem: A bacterial species has a surface that lacks pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that are easily recognized by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) on phagocytes. Which of the following complement-mediated functions is most important for efficient phagocytic clearance of this organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of B cells by C3d

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coating of the surface with C3b

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degranulation of mast cells by C5a

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of pores by C9 polymerization

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stabilization of the C3 convertase by properdin

explanation.summary: Opsonization by C3b is particularly important for clearing pathogens that lack PAMPs easily recognized by PRRs.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that some complement proteins coat an invading pathogen and are recognized by complement receptors on phagocytes, making phagocytosis more efficient. It specifically notes that opsonization is particularly important in clearing pathogens that do not have PAMPs easily recognized by PRRs; C3b and iC3b are good opsonins recognized by CR1 on phagocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3d helps activate B cells as part of immune modulation, not phagocytic clearance of a pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C5a-induced mast cell degranulation promotes inflammation but does not tag the pathogen for phagocyte recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C9 polymerization forms the membrane attack complex and causes direct lysis; it does not enhance phagocytic recognition of the microbe.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Properdin stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase but does not itself provide the phagocyte-recognized tag on the pathogen.

questions.stem: Which of the following complement fragments functions as an opsonin that is recognized by complement receptor 1 (CR1) on phagocytes?

explanation.summary: C3b and inactivated C3b (iC3b) are the complement opsonins recognized by CR1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that C3b and iC3b are good opsonins and are recognized by complement receptor 1 (CR1). The summary reiterates that opsonization is mediated by C3b and inactivated C3b (iC3b). Binding of bound C3b/iC3b by the phagocyte CR1 leads to phagocytosis and killing of the microbe.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3a is an anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation; it is released into solution rather than coating the pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C4a is a weak anaphylatoxin and is not recognized by CR1 as an opsonin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C5a is the most potent anaphylatoxin and a leukocyte chemoattractant, not a surface-bound opsonin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C9 polymerizes into the pore of the membrane attack complex and has no opsonic role.

questions.stem: In an experiment, purified C3a is injected intradermally into a healthy volunteer. Within minutes, localized redness and swelling develop at the injection site. Which of the following is the most direct mechanism of this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of immune complexes to erythrocyte CR1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of C5 into C5a and C5b at the site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Covalent deposition of C3b on endothelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Degranulation of mast cells with release of histamine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymerization of C9 into pores in endothelial membranes

explanation.summary: C3a is an anaphylatoxin that directly activates mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and TNF-alpha.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that C5a, C3a, and (to a lesser extent) C4a increase vascular permeability, adhesion molecule expression on the endothelium, and vascular smooth muscle contraction, and can induce degranulation of mast cells and basophils, raising histamine and TNF-alpha levels. Because administering these fragments mimics the effects of histamine, they are collectively termed anaphylatoxins; a local injection of C3a therefore produces histamine-mediated swelling and redness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocyte CR1 binds C3b-coated immune complexes for clearance, which is unrelated to a local anaphylatoxin response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C5 cleavage requires a C5 convertase; injected C3a acts directly on mast cells rather than through C5 cleavage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C3b, not C3a, covalently deposits on surfaces, and opsonization does not itself cause redness and swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C9 polymerization is the terminal step of MAC formation and requires C5b-C8 on a membrane; C3a does not initiate it.

questions.stem: Apart from its roles in pathogen destruction, complement modulates the adaptive immune response. Which of the following complement fragments regulates antibody responses by helping to activate B cells?

explanation.summary: C3d helps activate B cells and thereby regulates antibody responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Under immune system modulation, the brick lists B cell activation as a secondary function of complement and states that C3d, discussed later in the context of the adaptive immune system, regulates antibody responses by helping activate B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3a is an anaphylatoxin that promotes inflammation, not B cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C4b is a component of the classical and lectin C3 convertase, not a B cell co-activator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C5a is the most potent anaphylatoxin and recruits leukocytes; it is not the fragment that helps activate B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C9 forms the pore of the membrane attack complex and has no role in B cell activation.

questions.stem: During normal tissue turnover, large numbers of cells undergo apoptosis and must be cleared without provoking inflammation. Phagocytes remove the apoptotic remnants after complement components bind molecules displayed on the apoptotic cell surface. Which of the following pairs of complement components performs this binding?

explanation.summary: C1q and MBL bind surface molecules on apoptotic cells and fragments, allowing phagocyte complement receptors to clear the debris.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that complement can work with phagocytes to remove remnants of apoptosis: C1q and MBL bind molecules on the surface of apoptotic cells or cell fragments, and these complement components are then recognized by complement receptors on phagocytes, facilitating phagocytosis and clearance of the debris. It also notes that MBL binds mannose patterns found on apoptotic human cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C5a and C3a are soluble anaphylatoxins that promote inflammation; they do not tag apoptotic cells for clearance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C6 and C7 are terminal pathway components that join C5b to build the membrane attack complex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD55 and CD59 are host-cell inhibitors that protect cells from complement, not recognition molecules for apoptotic debris.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Factor B and Factor D generate the alternative pathway C3 convertase; they do not recognize apoptotic cells.

questions.stem: Erythrocytes from patients with rheumatoid arthritis are compared with erythrocytes from healthy volunteers. Which of the following findings on the patients' erythrocytes would best explain the buildup of immune complexes in the small vasculature that characterizes their disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent CD55 and CD59 on the surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent glycolipid anchors on the surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased C4b2b assembly on the surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased MAC deposition on the surface

explanation.summary: Patients with SLE and rheumatoid arthritis express erythrocyte CR1 at 20-50% lower rates than healthy volunteers, impairing immune complex clearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: CR1 on erythrocytes binds C3b-coated immune complexes so that phagocytes in the spleen and liver can strip and destroy them. The brick notes that SLE and rheumatoid arthritis are characterized by buildup of immune complexes in the small vasculature, and that several studies show these patients express CR1 at 20-50% lower rates than healthy volunteers, suggesting that CR1 deficiency may contribute to the pathology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of CD55 and CD59 is the defect in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria and causes erythrocyte lysis, not immune complex accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective glycolipid anchors cause loss of DAF and CD59 and produce PNH, not the reduced CR1 expression seen in autoimmune disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C4b2b is the classical C3 convertase; its assembly on erythrocytes is not the mechanism described for immune complex buildup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increased MAC deposition would cause hemolysis rather than impaired transport of immune complexes.

questions.stem: The classical, lectin, and alternative pathways are each initiated by different molecules, but all three converge on the formation of the same type of multimeric enzyme. Which of the following reactions does this shared enzyme catalyze?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cleavage of C3 into C3a and C3b

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleavage of C4 into C4a and C4b

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of C5 into C5a and C5b

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cleavage of Factor B into Ba and Bb

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymerization of C9 into a pore

explanation.summary: All activation pathways make a C3 convertase, whose function is to cleave C3 into C3a and C3b.
explanation.whyCorrect: One of the brick's 'rules of 3' is that all activation pathways make C3 convertase, a multimeric enzyme that cleaves complement component 3 into the fragments C3a and C3b. Although the classical/lectin convertase (C4b2b) and the alternative convertase (C3bBb) differ in composition, their function is the same: to convert C3 to C3a and C3b.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C4 is cleaved by C1s or the MASPs in the classical and lectin pathways, not by the convergent C3 convertase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C5 is cleaved by the C5 convertase, which forms only after C3b binds the C3 convertase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor B is cleaved by Factor D during alternative pathway activation, upstream of convertase formation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C9 polymerization is the final step of membrane attack complex assembly in the terminal pathway.

questions.stem: A researcher activates C3 in vitro and incubates it separately with beads coated with bacterial polysaccharide and beads coated with a purified host protein. Covalent attachment of the activated C3 fragment is detected on both types of bead. Which of the following properties of activated C3 best explains this observation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attachment to complement receptor 1 on the surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding to the Fc region of surface-bound antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exposure of a hydrophobic site that inserts into lipid bilayers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exposure of a reactive thioester that attaches to primary amines

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recognition of mannose residues by a lectin domain

explanation.summary: Activated C3 exposes a reactive thioester that lets it bind essentially any surface bearing a primary amine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick's clinical reasoning box explains that when C3 is activated it exposes a reactive thioester that allows the peptide to attach to any surface with a primary amine. Because primary amines are present in both proteins and polysaccharides, activated C3 can bind essentially any surface, which is why the cascade must be tightly regulated to avoid immunopathology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CR1 is a phagocyte and erythrocyte receptor that recognizes bound C3b; it is not present on the coated beads and does not explain covalent attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Binding antibody Fc regions is how C1q initiates the classical pathway; it would not explain attachment to an antibody-free protein bead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Exposure of a hydrophobic membrane-inserting site describes C7 within the C5bC6C7 complex, not activated C3.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mannose recognition through a lectin domain is the function of mannose-binding lectin in the lectin pathway.

questions.stem: C1 is a soluble protein complex whose C1q subunit binds two adjacent molecules of IgG on a pathogen surface. Following this binding event, which of the following subunits of the C1 complex cleaves C4 and C2 into their a and b fragments?

explanation.summary: C1q binding allows C1s to cleave C4 and C2, whose b fragments join to form the classical C3 convertase C4b2b.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes C1 as a soluble complex made of C1s, C1r, and C1q subunits. C1q is the recognition subunit that binds antibody or CRP, and C1q binding allows C1s to cleave C4 and C2 into a and b fragments; C4b and C2b then join to form C4b2b, the classical C3 convertase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1q is the subunit that binds antibody or CRP on the pathogen surface; it is not the protease that cleaves C4 and C2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C1r is a subunit of the C1 complex, but the brick identifies C1s as the subunit that cleaves C4 and C2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor D cleaves Factor B into Ba and Bb in the alternative pathway and has no role in C4 or C2 cleavage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MASP-2 cleaves C4 and C2 in the lectin pathway after MBL binds mannose; it is not part of the C1 complex.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man is hospitalized with pneumococcal pneumonia. Before a specific antibody response has developed, an acute phase reactant in his serum rises markedly, binds the bacterial surface, and engages C1q to trigger the classical complement pathway. Which of the following proteins is responsible?

explanation.summary: C-reactive protein, an acute phase reactant and opsonin, is one of the two clinically relevant ligands that C1q binds to activate the classical pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists two clinically relevant components on a pathogen surface that C1q can bind: C-reactive protein (CRP), described as an acute phase reactant and an opsonin, and the antibodies IgG and IgM. Figure 4's caption likewise notes that the classical C3 convertase is generated when C1q binds to antibody or CRP, so CRP can trigger the classical pathway even before antibody appears.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Factor B is an alternative pathway component that binds C3b and is cleaved by Factor D; it does not engage C1q.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haptoglobin is a plasma protein that binds free hemoglobin; it does not activate complement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannose-binding lectin initiates the lectin pathway through MASPs and does not act via C1q.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Properdin stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase and is not a C1q ligand.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is found to have a homozygous deletion of the gene encoding complement component C2, with no detectable C2 protein in his serum. Complement activation through which of the following would be expected to be impaired?

explanation.summary: C2 is required to build C4b2b, the shared C3 convertase of both the classical and lectin pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the classical pathway, C1s cleaves C4 and C2 so that C4b and C2b join to form the C3 convertase C4b2b. The brick emphasizes that the lectin pathway generates the very same convertase: after MBL binds, the MASPs cleave C2 and C4, and C4b binds C2b to make C4b2b. Without C2, neither pathway can assemble its C3 convertase, whereas the alternative pathway convertase (C3bBb) uses Factors B and D and remains intact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The alternative pathway is the one pathway that does not use C2 at all.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The alternative pathway builds its convertase from C3b, Factor B, and Factor D and does not require C2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lectin pathway does need C2, but the alternative pathway does not; the classical pathway is the other one affected.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lectin pathway is affected, but so is the classical pathway, because both depend on C4b2b.

questions.stem: A bacterium enters the bloodstream of a patient who has no antibody against it, and its surface displays no mannose-containing patterns. Nevertheless, its surface rapidly becomes coated with C3b. Which of the following initiating events best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of C1q to CRP on the surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of MBL to sugars on the surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of C5 by the terminal pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spontaneous tickover of C3 near the surface

explanation.summary: The alternative pathway is initiated by spontaneous hydrolysis (tickover) of C3, without antibody or lectin recognition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that C3 has a slow rate of tickover, or spontaneous water-mediated hydrolysis, and that this tickover initiates the alternative pathway. The resulting C3b fragment covalently binds the closest primary amine; Factor B then binds C3b and is cleaved by Factor D into Ba and Bb, generating the alternative C3 convertase C3bBb, which amplifies C3b deposition on the surface.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1q binding to CRP or antibody initiates the classical pathway, but the stem specifies the surface is not antibody-coated and describes a recognition-independent process.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MBL initiates the lectin pathway by binding mannose, which the stem states is absent from this surface.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C5 cleavage occurs downstream of C3b deposition and C5 convertase formation; it cannot be the initiating event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Properdin stabilizes the alternative convertase C3bBb, not C4b2b, and stabilization is not an initiating step.

questions.stem: In the alternative pathway, the C3 convertase C3bBb is stabilized on a pathogen surface by properdin. A second molecule of C3b then binds to this convertase. Which of the following enzyme complexes is generated by this binding event?

explanation.summary: Binding of a second C3b to the alternative C3 convertase creates the alternative pathway C5 convertase, C3b2Bb.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that properdin stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase and that if another molecule of C3b binds, it generates the alternative pathway C5 convertase (C3b2Bb). This parallels the general rule that C3b binds to the C3 convertase to form the C5 convertase, which cleaves C5 into C5a and C5b.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C3bBb is the alternative pathway C3 convertase that exists before the second C3b binds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C4b2b is the C3 convertase of the classical and lectin pathways, not an alternative pathway complex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C4b2b3b is the classical and lectin pathway C5 convertase, formed from C4b2b rather than from C3bBb.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C5bC6C7 is the initial terminal pathway complex that inserts into the membrane; it is formed after C5 cleavage, not by C3b binding a convertase.

questions.stem: Although it was discovered after the classical pathway, one of the three complement activation pathways is responsible for producing most of the C3b and 80-90% of the membrane attack complexes generated during an immune response. Which pathway is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All three activation pathways contribute equally

explanation.summary: The alternative pathway, despite its name, produces most of the C3b and 80-90% of the MAC.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the alternative pathway gets its name because it was discovered later and was thought to be an alternative to the classical pathway, yet it produces most of the C3b and 80-90% of the MAC. Its tickover-initiated, antibody-independent activation and the C3b-amplifying C3bBb convertase make it the dominant source of complement effector molecules.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick explicitly attributes the majority of C3b and 80-90% of MAC to the alternative pathway, not an equal split.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The classical pathway was discovered first but is not the source of most C3b or MAC.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lectin pathway shares the C4b2b convertase with the classical pathway and is not described as the dominant producer of C3b or MAC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The terminal pathway is the shared MAC-assembly stage downstream of all three activation pathways, not an activation pathway itself.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl has had three episodes of severe, invasive Streptococcus pneumoniae infection despite complete vaccination. Her serum lyses IgM-sensitized sheep erythrocytes normally in the CH50 assay, but produces no lysis in the AH50 assay. Deficiency of which of the following proteins is most likely?

explanation.summary: A normal CH50 with an absent AH50 localizes the defect to a component unique to the alternative pathway, such as Factor D.
explanation.whyCorrect: The CH50 tests the classical pathway, whereas the AH50 tests the alternative pathway by including inhibitors of the classical and lectin pathways. Normal lysis in the CH50 means C1, C4, C2, C3, and the terminal components are intact, so the absent AH50 must reflect loss of a protein used only by the alternative pathway. Factor D, which cleaves Factor B into Ba and Bb to form the C3bBb convertase, is the only alternative-pathway-specific protein listed; its loss leaves the child susceptible to encapsulated bacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1q deficiency would reduce the CH50, which is normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C2 is part of C4b2b, the classical and lectin C3 convertase; its deficiency would reduce the CH50.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C4 is used by the classical and lectin pathways; its loss would lower the CH50 rather than selectively abolish the AH50.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MBL deficiency affects only the lectin pathway, which is inhibited in the AH50 assay and not measured by either test described.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man reports several years of recurrent episodes of severe abdominal pain, nausea, and diarrhea lasting a few days, and one prior episode of lip swelling that did not itch. His father had similar episodes. Hereditary angioedema is suspected. Which of the following laboratory patterns would most strongly support this diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased AH50 with a normal CH50

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased C3 with normal C4 and C1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased C4 with normal C1 and C3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased CD55 and CD59 on erythrocytes

explanation.summary: In C1-INH deficiency, C1 and C3 levels are normal, but C4 below 50% of normal is strongly suggestive of hereditary angioedema.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that C1-INH deficiency, responsible for the vast majority of HAE cases, is diagnosed by a decreased amount or function of C1-INH; C1 and C3 levels are normal, but C4 levels below 50% of normal are strongly suggestive of HAE. Unopposed C1 activity consumes C4, explaining the pattern. The recurrent non-itchy swelling with gastrointestinal symptoms and a family history fits HAE.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A low AH50 with a normal CH50 indicates an alternative pathway defect, which is unrelated to C1-INH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C3 is normal in HAE; a low C3 would point toward a shared-component deficiency rather than C1-INH deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of CD55 and CD59 on flow cytometry is the diagnostic finding of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not HAE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reduced haptoglobin reflects intravascular hemolysis, as in PNH; it is not part of the HAE picture, and C4 would be low rather than normal.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with known hereditary angioedema presents to the emergency department with rapidly progressive swelling of the tongue and throat and increasing difficulty breathing. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this acute attack?

explanation.summary: Acute HAE attacks are treated with recombinant C1-INH, inhibitors of bradykinin signaling, or plasma infusion to replace the lost C1-INH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients with acute attacks from HAE can be treated with recombinant C1-INH, inhibitors of bradykinin signaling, or plasma infusion, which replaces the lost C1-INH. Laryngeal swelling is described as the most dangerous manifestation because it can limit the ability to breathe, so rapid replacement of the deficient inhibitor is the appropriate intervention.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antihistamines do not improve HAE swelling, which is bradykinin-mediated rather than histamine-mediated; this is a distinguishing feature from allergic reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eculizumab blocks C5 cleavage and is used for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, not for bradykinin-mediated angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, which slows bradykinin degradation and is contraindicated in HAE; it would worsen the attack.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prophylactic antibiotics are used for recurrent infections in terminal complement deficiency and have no role in treating angioedema.

questions.stem: Attacks of hereditary angioedema are usually self-limiting but can last several days and involve multiple sites at once. Swelling at which of the following sites is the most dangerous during an attack?

explanation.summary: Laryngeal swelling is the most dangerous manifestation of HAE because it can compromise the ability to breathe.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that HAE swelling can be visible, such as of the lips, or cause non-specific symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and gastrointestinal pain, but that laryngeal swelling is the most dangerous, potentially limiting the ability to breathe.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Facial swelling, as shown in the brick's figure, is dramatic but does not by itself obstruct breathing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Swelling of the hands is uncomfortable but not life-threatening.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intestinal wall swelling causes nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, but it is not described as the most dangerous site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lip swelling is a visible and disfiguring manifestation but does not threaten the airway.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry of erythrocytes from a patient with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria shows loss of two glycolipid-anchored complement inhibitors, CD55 and CD59. Which of the following best describes the normal protective function of CD59?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks formation of the C3 convertase on the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks the enzymatic activity of the C1 complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleaves Factor B into the Ba and Bb fragments

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits formation of the membrane attack complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase

explanation.summary: CD59 is a membrane inhibitor that prevents MAC formation, whereas DAF (CD55) blocks C3 convertase formation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes decay-accelerating factor (DAF, CD55) as a membrane-bound protein that blocks C3 convertase formation and is anchored by a glycolipid. Deficiency of that glycolipid causes loss of both DAF and a less critical complement inhibitor, CD59, which inhibits formation of the MAC. When both are lost, MACs form on erythrocytes exposed to complement, producing the hemolysis of PNH.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking C3 convertase formation is the function of DAF (CD55), the other glycolipid-anchored inhibitor lost in PNH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking C1 activity is the function of the soluble C1 esterase inhibitor, whose deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleaving Factor B is the function of Factor D in the alternative pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stabilizing the alternative C3 convertase is the function of properdin, which promotes rather than inhibits complement activity.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria has ongoing intravascular lysis of erythrocytes by membrane attack complexes, releasing free hemoglobin into the plasma. The free hemoglobin is bound with high affinity by a plasma protein whose serum level is therefore typically reduced in this disease. Which of the following is this protein?

explanation.summary: Haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin with high affinity and is typically reduced in PNH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PNH is confirmed by flow cytometry showing low surface expression of DAF/CD55 and CD59, and that blood levels of haptoglobin, a plasma protein that binds with high affinity to free hemoglobin, are typically reduced as well. Ongoing MAC-mediated lysis of circulating erythrocytes releases hemoglobin that consumes haptoglobin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C-reactive protein is an acute phase reactant and opsonin that binds pathogen surfaces and C1q, not free hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C1 esterase inhibitor regulates C1 and bradykinin release and is unrelated to hemoglobin binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannose-binding lectin binds mannose on pathogens and apoptotic cells, not hemoglobin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Properdin stabilizes the alternative C3 convertase; it does not bind hemoglobin.

questions.stem: Five unrelated children each have a complete inherited deficiency of a single complement protein. Which of the following children is expected to have the most severe susceptibility to infections with encapsulated bacteria?

explanation.summary: Deficiencies in components shared by all pathways, such as C3, produce a more severe presentation than deficiencies confined to a single activation pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that early complement deficiencies increase susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria through loss of opsonization by C3b, reduced inflammation by C3a and C5a, and reduced MAC formation. It then states that deficiencies in shared components, such as C3, result in a more severe presentation than deficiencies in only one of the activation pathways, because every pathway must cleave C3 to generate these effectors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C1q is used only by the classical pathway; the lectin and alternative pathways can still generate C3b and MAC.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C2 is required by the classical and lectin pathways, but the alternative pathway, which produces most C3b, remains intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Factor B is specific to the alternative pathway; the classical and lectin pathways can still activate C3.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MBL deficiency affects only the lectin pathway, leaving the classical and alternative pathways functional.

questions.stem: Before conjugate vaccines were introduced, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningitidis were among the most common causes of severe invasive infections in children. Conjugate vaccines reduced these infections primarily through which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acceleration of spontaneous C3 tickover on the bacterial capsule surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generation of high-affinity antibodies against the capsule polysaccharide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased hepatic synthesis of complement proteins during inflammation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Induction of properdin to stabilize the alternative pathway C3 convertase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of CR1 on circulating erythrocytes for complex clearance

explanation.summary: Conjugate vaccines generate high-affinity antibodies against capsular polysaccharide that opsonize the bacteria and drive the classical and terminal complement pathways.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that conjugate vaccines allow the generation of high-affinity antibodies directed against the capsule polysaccharide. These antibodies can bind encapsulated pathogens directly, opsonizing them, and are also critical for optimal function of the classical and terminal complement pathways, which is why terminal complement deficiency leaves vaccinated patients still vulnerable.

whyWrongByChoice.A: C3 tickover is a spontaneous, antibody-independent process and is not altered by vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vaccination does not increase hepatic complement synthesis; complement proteins rise as acute phase reactants during inflammation, not in response to vaccines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vaccines do not act by inducing properdin; properdin is a constitutive stabilizer of the alternative C3 convertase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CR1 expression on erythrocytes is involved in immune complex clearance and is not the mechanism of vaccine protection.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is found on genetic testing to have a complete deficiency of C1q. Which of the following best explains the association between her complement deficiency and her autoimmune disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excessive membrane attack complex formation on host cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of C3d-dependent B cell activation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Overproduction of the anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced clearance of apoptotic cells and immune complexes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unopposed release of bradykinin from plasma

explanation.summary: Loss of C1q or C3 impairs clearance of apoptotic cells and immune complexes, leaving an overabundance of self-antigens that drives autoimmunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that loss of C1q or C3 is associated with autoimmune conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus, and that this effect is believed to be due to a reduced ability to clear apoptotic cells and immune complexes, leading to an overabundance of self-antigens. C1q normally binds apoptotic cell surfaces for phagocyte clearance, and C1q-initiated classical activation generates the C3b that coats immune complexes for CR1-mediated removal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Excessive MAC formation on host cells is the mechanism of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria; C1q deficiency reduces, rather than increases, complement activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: C3d-mediated B cell activation is a downstream modulatory function; the brick attributes the lupus association to impaired clearance of self-antigen sources, not to failed B cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: C1q deficiency reduces classical pathway activation and therefore would not cause overproduction of anaphylatoxins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unopposed bradykinin release results from C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency and causes hereditary angioedema, not lupus.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old boy is brought in for a red, warm swelling at the base of the umbilicus. His parents note that his umbilical cord did not fall off until 30 days of age. Despite the obvious inflammation, the lesion contains almost no pus. A CBC shows leukocytosis with marked neutrophilia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Omphalitis with delayed cord separation, pus-free infection, and neutrophilia is the classic presentation of leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 (LAD-I).
explanation.whyCorrect: In LAD-I, mutations in CD18 prevent neutrophil integrins (LFA-1) from mediating firm adhesion, so neutrophils cannot leave the vessels to enter tissue. Sites of infection are therefore devoid of pus even when inflamed, and neutrophils pile up in the blood, causing leukocytosis and neutrophilia. Delayed umbilical cord separation (around 30 days versus the normal ~15 days) and omphalitis are classic early signs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chediak-Higashi syndrome presents with partial albinism, giant granules in leukocytes, and bleeding, not with delayed cord separation and pus-free omphalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic granulomatous disease produces abundant granulomas and abscesses with catalase-positive organisms; neutrophils still enter tissue, so infections are not pus-free.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Physiologic neutrophilia does not cause an infected, pus-poor umbilical stump or delayed cord separation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terminal complement deficiency classically causes recurrent Neisseria infections, not neonatal omphalitis with delayed cord separation.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry on the infant from the previous scenario shows less than 2% expression of CD18 on his leukocytes, and CD11a is also low. A defect in which of the following processes best explains why his sites of infection lack pus?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophil firm adhesion and transmigration into tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oxygen-dependent killing and reactive oxygen species generation

explanation.summary: LFA-1 is a heterodimer of CD18 and CD11a; loss of CD18 blocks integrin-mediated firm adhesion and diapedesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because CD11a expression depends on CD18, a CD18 mutation leaves leukocytes lacking both. Without functional LFA-1, neutrophils cannot bind ICAMs to firmly adhere and then transmigrate across the endothelium, so they never reach the tissue to form pus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement opsonization is not encoded by CD18 and is not the defect here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Defective lysosomal trafficking is the mechanism of Chediak-Higashi syndrome (LYST mutation).
whyWrongByChoice.D: Defective reactive oxygen species generation is the mechanism of chronic granulomatous disease, not LAD-I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selectin-mediated rolling is intact in LAD-I; the block is at the later integrin-dependent firm-adhesion step.

questions.stem: During recruitment of neutrophils to an inflamed tissue, the first low-affinity, transient interaction that slows circulating neutrophils into a roll along the endothelium is mediated by which of the following pairs of molecules?

explanation.summary: Slow rolling (tethering) is driven by low-affinity selectin binding to sialyl-Lewis X carbohydrate ligands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endothelial E- and P-selectins bind the sialyl-Lewis X ligand on neutrophils with low affinity. These interactions are constantly formed and broken, disrupting the neutrophil's flow and causing it to roll slowly along the endothelium as the first step of recruitment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CXCL8 signaling upregulates integrins but does not itself tether the neutrophil to the endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrin binding to adhesion molecules produces firm adhesion, which follows rolling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LFA-1 binding ICAM-1 mediates the later step of firm adhesion, which arrests rolling rather than initiating it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PECAM-1 homophilic binding mediates diapedesis, the final transmigration step, not initial rolling.

questions.stem: A rolling neutrophil is exposed to the chemokine CXCL8 (IL-8) at a site of infection, which increases the affinity of LFA-1 for endothelial ICAM-1. What is the immediate result of this integrin-ICAM interaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Firm adhesion that stops the neutrophil from rolling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fusion of the phagosome with lysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate release of reactive oxygen species into the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Initiation of tethering and slow rolling

choices.label: E
choices.text: Return of the neutrophil to the circulating pool

explanation.summary: Integrin-ICAM binding produces firm adhesion, arresting the rolling neutrophil on the endothelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once the neutrophil is slowed, CXCL8/IL-8 upregulates integrins such as LFA-1 and increases their affinity for ICAM-1 and VCAM-1. TNF-alpha and IL-1 raise ICAM expression on the endothelium. The resulting integrin-ICAM interaction mediates firm adhesion and prevents further rolling.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Phagosome-lysosome fusion is a step of intracellular killing, unrelated to endothelial adhesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The respiratory burst occurs inside phagosomes during killing, not upon adhesion to endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tethering and slow rolling occur earlier and are mediated by selectins, not integrin-ICAM binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Firm adhesion holds the neutrophil in place for transmigration; it does not send it back into circulation.

questions.stem: After firmly adhering to the endothelium, a neutrophil squeezes between adjacent endothelial cells to enter the infected tissue. This transmigration step, called diapedesis, is chiefly mediated by which of the following molecules?

explanation.summary: Diapedesis (migration/extravasation) is mediated primarily by PECAM-1 on both neutrophils and endothelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: PECAM-1 is an adhesion molecule found on neutrophils and at endothelial junctions. Its homophilic interactions guide the firmly adhered neutrophil between endothelial cells and into the tissue, following chemokine gradients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase is a microbial (and human) enzyme that degrades hydrogen peroxide; it plays no role in diapedesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: E-selectin mediates the earlier rolling step, not transmigration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase is an enzyme of intracellular oxygen-dependent killing, not a recruitment molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sialyl-Lewis X is the selectin ligand used during rolling, not diapedesis.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with silvery-blond hair, very pale skin, and photophobia has had repeated Staphylococcus aureus skin infections and bruises easily. A peripheral blood smear shows large, abnormal granules within her neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Partial albinism, recurrent infections, bleeding, and giant granules in granulocytes are the hallmark tetrad of Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chediak-Higashi syndrome results from a LYST mutation that disrupts lysosome and vesicle trafficking. This produces partial oculocutaneous albinism (giant melanosomes), recurrent pyogenic infections (defective neutrophil, CTL, and NK lysosomes), bleeding (defective platelet granules), and the classic giant azurophilic inclusion bodies in granulocytes on smear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic granulomatous disease causes catalase-positive infections and granulomas, not albinism or giant granules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LAD-I causes pus-free infections and delayed cord separation but not albinism or giant granules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infections without albinism or granule abnormalities.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Isolated tyrosinase-negative albinism causes hypopigmentation alone, not recurrent infections, bleeding, or giant granules.

questions.stem: The disorder affecting the child in the previous scenario is caused by a mutation in the LYST gene. Which cellular process is primarily disrupted by this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assembly of the NADPH oxidase complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expression of the integrin subunit CD18

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of the membrane attack complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lysosome and vesicle trafficking and fusion

explanation.summary: LYST (lysosomal trafficking regulator) governs the trafficking and fusion of lysosomes and other vesicles.
explanation.whyCorrect: LYST regulates vesicle trafficking and fusion. When it is mutated, lysosomes and related vesicles (including melanosomes and platelet granules) fail to move and fuse normally, producing the immunodeficiency, albinism, bleeding, and neurologic defects of Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Defective NADPH oxidase assembly underlies chronic granulomatous disease, not Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of CD18 expression causes LAD-I, a different disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure to form the membrane attack complex reflects terminal complement deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Defective selectin ligand synthesis impairs rolling but is not the LYST defect.

questions.stem: A child with Chediak-Higashi syndrome develops easy bruising and prolonged bleeding after minor cuts. This bleeding tendency is best explained by a defect in which of the following?

explanation.summary: Platelets contain granules that promote clotting; in Chediak-Higashi syndrome these granules are defective.
explanation.whyCorrect: Platelet granules are vesicles containing molecules important for clotting. Because LYST regulates vesicle function, platelet granules are defective in Chediak-Higashi syndrome, leading to a bleeding tendency and prolonged bleeding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A and is unrelated to the LYST vesicle defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A structural collagen/vascular defect (as in some connective tissue diseases) is not the CHS bleeding mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency reflects a coagulation-factor problem, not defective platelet granules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: von Willebrand factor deficiency is a separate primary hemostatic disorder, not the mechanism in CHS.

questions.stem: A boy with Chediak-Higashi syndrome who has not received a hematopoietic stem cell transplant becomes acutely ill with fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia; biopsy shows organ infiltration by activated macrophages and lymphocytes. More than 80% of untreated CHS patients develop this life-threatening complication. It is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Untreated Chediak-Higashi syndrome frequently progresses to hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).
explanation.whyCorrect: Without a transplant, more than 80% of CHS patients develop HLH, a hyper-inflammatory state in which lymphocytes and histiocytes (macrophages) invade organs, causing multi-organ failure. HLH typically produces pancytopenia (reduced red cells, white cells, and platelets).

whyWrongByChoice.A: DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy, not the hyper-inflammatory histiocytic syndrome described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Graft-versus-host disease requires a prior transplant of immune cells; this patient has not been transplanted.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amyloidosis is a slow protein-deposition disorder and does not explain this acute inflammatory picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CHS does not transform into chronic granulomatous disease; they are distinct genetic disorders.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has had recurrent abscesses growing Staphylococcus aureus and Serratia marcescens and now has an Aspergillus pneumonia with granuloma formation on biopsy. Which of the following tests best confirms the suspected diagnosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral smear for giant granulocyte inclusions

explanation.summary: Deep-seated infections with catalase-positive organisms and granulomas suggest chronic granulomatous disease, confirmed by the DHR test.
explanation.whyCorrect: The DHR flow cytometry test measures the ability of phagocytes to reduce dihydrorhodamine to fluorescent rhodamine via NADPH oxidase. Because CGD phagocytes lack functional NADPH oxidase, they produce little or no rhodamine. (The older nitroblue tetrazolium test measures the same defect.)

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD18 flow cytometry diagnoses LAD-I, which causes pus-free infections rather than granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LYST genetic testing confirms Chediak-Higashi syndrome, not chronic granulomatous disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Giant granulocyte inclusions on smear point to Chediak-Higashi syndrome, not CGD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A CH50 assay screens for complement deficiencies, which present with Neisseria infections, not catalase-positive abscesses.

questions.stem: Patients with chronic granulomatous disease are especially prone to infection by catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. Which of the following best explains this specific susceptibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Catalase-positive microbes are resistant to complement-mediated lysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Catalase-positive microbes are strictly intracellular and evade antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: Catalase-positive microbes block selectin-mediated rolling of neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Catalase-positive microbes degrade their own hydrogen peroxide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Catalase-positive microbes inhibit the LYST protein in host cells

explanation.summary: Catalase-positive organisms neutralize their own hydrogen peroxide, removing the peroxide that CGD neutrophils would otherwise borrow for killing.
explanation.whyCorrect: CGD neutrophils lack NADPH oxidase, but their myeloperoxidase can still convert hydrogen peroxide made by invading bacteria into hypochlorite. Catalase-positive species destroy their own hydrogen peroxide, so they deprive myeloperoxidase of substrate and survive, whereas catalase-negative organisms effectively supply the peroxide needed to kill them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistance to complement lysis characterizes some encapsulated organisms and does not explain the CGD-specific catalase link.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Several catalase-positive CGD pathogens (e.g., Aspergillus, S. aureus) are not strictly intracellular, so this is not the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CGD does not impair selectin-mediated rolling; the defect is in oxygen-dependent killing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LYST is the Chediak-Higashi protein and is unrelated to microbial catalase.

questions.stem: Chronic granulomatous disease most commonly results from a defect in which enzyme, and what is its most typical inheritance pattern?

explanation.summary: CGD is most often caused by X-linked recessive mutations in NADPH oxidase.
explanation.whyCorrect: NADPH oxidase begins the respiratory burst by generating superoxide from molecular oxygen; if it is deficient, the entire oxidative burst fails. Most cases of CGD are X-linked recessive, which is why males (with a single X chromosome) are affected far more often than females.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase is not the deficient host enzyme in CGD; catalase is relevant as a microbial virulence factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is a distinct, usually milder disorder and is not the most common cause of CGD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The enzyme is correct, but CGD is characteristically X-linked recessive, not autosomal dominant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superoxide dismutase is not the defective enzyme in CGD, and its loss does not define the disease.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old boy has had three soft-tissue infections since birth, and his physician suspects an inborn error of immunity. His parents ask how this differs from the immunodeficiency their uncle developed after chemotherapy. Which of the following best distinguishes an inborn error of immunity from a secondary immunodeficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caused by pathogens rather than by genetic mutations

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital rather than acquired later in life

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inherited in an X-linked rather than an autosomal pattern

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restricted to innate components rather than adaptive components

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uniformly fatal rather than variable in severity

explanation.summary: Inborn errors of immunity (primary immunodeficiencies) are present at birth, whereas acquired (secondary) immunodeficiencies develop at some point after birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: IEIs are inherited immunodeficiencies present at birth. They differ from acquired, or secondary, immunodeficiencies specifically in timing: acquired immunodeficiencies develop after birth (for example, following chemotherapy), whereas an IEI is a defect the child is born with.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IEIs are caused by genetic mutations, not by pathogens; it is secondary immunodeficiencies that may follow external insults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inheritance patterns vary among IEIs: LAD-I and CHS are autosomal recessive, while CGD is typically X-linked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IEIs can affect either the innate or the adaptive immune system; this brick focuses on innate IEIs, but the category is not limited to them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IEIs vary greatly in severity and presentation depending on the mutation; they are not uniformly fatal.

questions.stem: A splinter breaks the skin barrier of a 30-year-old woman and introduces bacteria. Pattern recognition receptors on sentinel cells recognize PAMPs and DAMPs, leading to the production of cytokines and chemokines. Which of the following best describes the primary role of the chemokines produced in this response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activate tissue-resident cells such as mast cells and macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attract circulating leukocytes such as neutrophils to the site of infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fuse lysosomes with the phagosome to digest ingested microbes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generate superoxide and hypochlorite inside the phagolysosome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recognize PAMPs and DAMPs on the surface of the invading bacteria

explanation.summary: Chemokines attract circulating leukocytes to the site of infection, whereas cytokines activate tissue-resident cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: During inflammation, PRR recognition of PAMPs and DAMPs drives production of cytokines and chemokines. Cytokines activate tissue-resident cells like mast cells and macrophages, and chemokines attract circulating leukocytes like neutrophils to the site of infection, where adhesion molecules then let them enter tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation of tissue-resident mast cells and macrophages is the role of cytokines, not chemokines.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lysosome-phagosome fusion is a step of intracellular killing regulated by proteins such as LYST, not by chemokines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Generation of reactive oxygen species is the function of NADPH oxidase and downstream enzymes in the respiratory burst, not chemokines.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Recognition of PAMPs and DAMPs is performed by pattern recognition receptors, which are upstream of chemokine production.

questions.stem: A researcher measures adhesion molecules on resting vascular endothelial cells and finds two of them expressed constitutively at low levels; their expression rises sharply when the cells are exposed to inflammatory signals, allowing them to capture passing neutrophils with low affinity. Which of the following pairs of molecules did the researcher most likely measure?

explanation.summary: Endothelial cells constitutively express E-selectin and P-selectin at low levels, and inflammation increases their expression to begin slowing neutrophils.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils travel through larger vessels at about a meter per second and must first slow down to leave the circulation. Endothelial cells constitutively express two adhesion molecules, E-selectin and P-selectin, at low levels; inflammation increases their expression, and selectin ligands on neutrophils bind them with low affinity to mediate slow rolling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD11a and CD18 are the subunits of the neutrophil integrin LFA-1, not endothelial molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CXCL8 and TNF-alpha are chemokine/cytokine signals that regulate adhesion, not adhesion molecules themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LFA-1 (which contains CD18) is a leukocyte integrin expressed on neutrophils, not on endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PECAM-1 is on both cells but mediates diapedesis, and sialyl-Lewis X is the ligand on the neutrophil, not an endothelial capture molecule.

questions.stem: A healthy 22-year-old man has blood drawn for a research study immediately after a vigorous 5-km run. His absolute neutrophil count is above the reference range. A repeat sample drawn the next morning at rest is normal. He has no fever, infection, or history of immunodeficiency. Which of the following best explains the initial finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute increase in bone marrow neutrophil production and release

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytokine-driven release of stored neutrophils from the lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exercise-induced rise in endothelial selectin expression and rolling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shift of the marginating neutrophil pool into the circulating pool

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transient loss of integrin-mediated firm adhesion to the endothelium

explanation.summary: Acute stress or exercise moves marginating neutrophils back into the circulating pool, producing transient neutrophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: At homeostasis roughly half of blood neutrophils are circulating and half are marginating (rolling on endothelium or moving into tissues). Stimuli such as acute stress or exercise cause the marginating pool to move back into the circulating pool, so a blood sample transiently shows a higher-than-normal neutrophil count that resolves at rest.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow production cannot rise within minutes of a run; the change reflects redistribution of existing neutrophils, not new production.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neutrophils are not stored in and released from lymph nodes; the reservoir that shifts is the marginating pool along the endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increased selectin expression would promote rolling and margination, which would lower rather than raise the circulating count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Loss of firm adhesion is the pathologic mechanism of LAD-I, which produces persistent neutrophilia with pus-poor infections, not a transient count in a healthy runner.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is stung by a bee on the forearm. Within minutes the site becomes red, warm, and swollen as mast cells degranulate. Beyond producing swelling, the histamine released at this site contributes to neutrophil recruitment by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding directly to sialyl-Lewis X on the surface of circulating neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Generating superoxide and hydrogen peroxide within the neutrophil phagolysosome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increasing vascular permeability and endothelial adhesion molecule expression

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mediating homophilic PECAM-1 binding at endothelial cell junctions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Raising the affinity of neutrophil LFA-1 integrin for endothelial ICAM-1

explanation.summary: Histamine, like IL-1 and C5a, induces increased vascular permeability and adhesion molecule expression that allow leukocytes to enter tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytokines like IL-1, complement components like C5a, and histamine released from mast cells can all induce increased vascular permeability and adhesion molecule expression on the endothelium. These adhesion molecules are what then allow leukocytes to slow, adhere, and enter the tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Sialyl-Lewis X is bound by endothelial selectins, not by histamine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Superoxide is generated by NADPH oxidase during the respiratory burst inside the neutrophil, unrelated to histamine signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PECAM-1 homophilic binding mediates diapedesis; histamine does not itself act as an adhesion molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increasing LFA-1 affinity for ICAMs is the action of IL-8 (CXCL8), not histamine.

questions.stem: In an in vitro flow chamber, endothelial cells are pretreated with TNF-alpha and IL-1, and neutrophils flowing over them are exposed to CXCL8. Compared with untreated controls, which of the following combinations of changes best accounts for the increased firm adhesion observed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased ICAM expression on endothelium and increased selectin affinity on neutrophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased ICAM expression on endothelium and increased LFA-1 affinity on neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased LFA-1 expression on endothelium and increased ICAM affinity on neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased PECAM-1 expression on endothelium and decreased LFA-1 affinity on neutrophils

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased sialyl-Lewis X on endothelium and increased selectin expression on neutrophils

explanation.summary: TNF-alpha and IL-1 raise endothelial ICAM expression, while IL-8 raises the affinity of neutrophil LFA-1 for ICAMs; together they produce firm adhesion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once neutrophils slow down, cytokines and chemokines like CXCL8/IL-8 cause them to upregulate integrins such as LFA-1 and increase the affinity of LFA-1 for ICAMs. On the endothelial side, TNF-alpha, IL-1, and other signals increase ICAM expression. The resulting integrin-ICAM interactions mediate firm adhesion and stop further rolling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TNF-alpha and IL-1 increase, not decrease, ICAM expression, and firm adhesion depends on integrins rather than selectin affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The molecules are on the wrong cells: LFA-1 is the neutrophil integrin and ICAM-1/VCAM-1 are on the endothelium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PECAM-1 mediates the later diapedesis step, and CXCL8 increases rather than decreases LFA-1 affinity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sialyl-Lewis X is the ligand on neutrophils and selectins are on endothelium; this reversed pairing describes neither cell correctly.

questions.stem: A neutrophil has completed diapedesis and is now within the interstitium of an infected wound. Which of the following sets of signals directs its movement toward the invading microbes once it is inside the tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chemokines, complement fragments, and bacterial products

choices.label: B
choices.text: E-selectin, P-selectin, and sialyl-Lewis X on the endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and the LFA-1 integrin on neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: PECAM-1 on neutrophils and on endothelial cell junctions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hypochlorite from the burst

explanation.summary: Inside the tissue, neutrophils follow gradients of chemokines, complement fragments, and bacterial products to reach the pathogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Firmly adhered neutrophils cross the endothelium by following chemokine gradients. Once inside the tissue, chemokines, complement fragments, and even bacterial products continue to guide them to the site of infection, where phagocytosis and killing occur.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Selectins and sialyl-Lewis X mediate the initial rolling on endothelium, before the neutrophil has left the vessel.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ICAMs and LFA-1 mediate firm adhesion on the vessel wall, not navigation within tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PECAM-1 mediates the transmigration step itself, which this neutrophil has already completed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive oxygen species are products of the respiratory burst used to kill ingested microbes, not guidance cues.

questions.stem: Flow cytometry on a 6-week-old infant with omphalitis and neutrophilia shows CD18 expression on leukocytes comparable to the negative control. Both parents are healthy; flow cytometry shows normal CD18 expression on the leukocytes of each parent. Which of the following best explains these family findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance arising from a de novo mutation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance in both parents

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance with both parents as heterozygous carriers

choices.label: E
choices.text: X-linked recessive inheritance with the mother as the sole carrier

explanation.summary: LAD-I is typically autosomal recessive; parents with normal CD18 expression who have an affected child are both carriers.
explanation.whyCorrect: LAD-I is caused by CD18 mutations that are typically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. In the flow cytometry shown for such a family, the patient's cells have low CD18 expression while both parents show normal expression, which confirms that both parents are carriers of the autosomal recessive allele.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A de novo dominant mutation would not require carrier parents, and LAD-I is not a dominant disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LAD-I is recessive; normal CD18 expression in the parents reflects heterozygous carrier status, not incomplete penetrance of a dominant allele.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defect is a genetic loss of CD18 present from birth, not an acquired condition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: LAD-I is autosomal recessive, not X-linked; X-linked inheritance is characteristic of most CGD cases.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has severe periodontal disease with gingival inflammation, recurrent skin infections, and a surgical incision from 6 weeks ago that has still not healed. Cultures from infected sites grow bacteria, yet the sites produce little pus. His white blood cell count is 42,000/mm3 with a marked neutrophil predominance. Which of the following best explains his elevated white blood cell count?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent NADPH oxidase drives compensatory marrow hyperplasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial catalase stimulates neutrophil release from the marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Defective lysosomal fusion prolongs neutrophil survival in the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of selectin ligands prevents neutrophil apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neutrophils cannot exit the vasculature and accumulate in the blood

explanation.summary: In LAD-I, neutrophils are produced normally but cannot leave the circulation, so they accumulate as leukocytosis with neutrophilia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mucosal bacterial infections of the skin, gingiva, and lung, periodontal disease, poor wound healing, and pus-poor infection sites are the clinical picture of LAD-I. Because CD18-deficient neutrophils cannot firmly adhere and enter tissues, the neutrophils produced by the bone marrow remain in the blood, producing leukocytosis from increased neutrophil counts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NADPH oxidase deficiency (CGD) impairs killing after neutrophils reach tissue; it does not cause pus-poor infections or this degree of neutrophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase is a microbial enzyme that protects microbes from the respiratory burst; it does not signal the marrow to release neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Defective lysosome trafficking is the CHS mechanism and is associated with neutropenia, not the leukocytosis seen here.
