whyWrongByChoice.D: The LAD-I defect is loss of the integrin subunit CD18, not selectin ligands, and the count rises from retention in blood rather than from blocked apoptosis.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl is diagnosed with LAD-I after flow cytometry shows CD18 expression on less than 2% of her leukocytes. She has already been hospitalized twice for soft-tissue infections. Her parents ask what treatment offers a long-term solution. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment?

explanation.summary: Severe LAD-I (near-absent CD18) can be fatal before age 2 and should be treated with hematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplant.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe cases of LAD-I can lead to death before 2 years of age and should be treated by hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT, also known as bone marrow transplant). Because leukocytes originate in the marrow, HSCT replaces the CD18-deficient neutrophils with functional ones and is discussed as the long-term solution for the infant in the brick's case.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G-CSF is given in Chediak-Higashi syndrome to correct neutropenia; LAD-I patients already have neutrophilia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prophylactic antibiotics with careful antibiotic use are appropriate for moderate loss of CD18 expression (2-30% of normal), not as definitive therapy for near-absent expression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing infected tissue treats one infection; it does not correct the underlying inability of neutrophils to enter tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IFN-gamma is used for moderate chronic granulomatous disease, not for LAD-I.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy with recurrent gingival and skin infections that produce little pus is found on flow cytometry to have CD18 expression at approximately 20% of normal. He is growing well and has never required intensive care. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor with prophylactic antibiotics

choices.label: B
choices.text: Observation without antibiotics until CD18 falls below 2%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prophylactic antibiotics with granulocyte transfusions as needed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type II interferon (IFN-gamma) with prophylactic antibiotics

explanation.summary: Moderate LAD-I (2-30% of normal CD18 expression) may be managed with prophylactic antibiotics, careful antibiotic use during infections, and granulocyte transfusions.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD18 mutations vary in their effect on expression and function. Moderate loss of CD18 expression, defined as 2-30% of normal, may be treatable with prophylactic antibiotics, careful antibiotic use during infections, and granulocyte transfusions, whereas HSCT is reserved for severe cases that can be fatal before age 2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G-CSF corrects neutropenia in Chediak-Higashi syndrome; LAD-I patients have neutrophilia, not neutropenia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Even moderate LAD-I carries a high risk of mucosal bacterial infections and warrants prophylaxis; waiting for expression to fall is not a recognized strategy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IFN-gamma is used for moderate chronic granulomatous disease, not for LAD-I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSCT is indicated for severe LAD-I; a patient with 20% expression and a moderate course may be managed conservatively.

questions.stem: A genetic counselor is explaining to a family the inheritance of two innate inborn errors of immunity: Chediak-Higashi syndrome and chronic granulomatous disease. Which of the following statements correctly contrasts their typical inheritance patterns?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both CHS and CGD are autosomal recessive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both CHS and CGD are typically X-linked

choices.label: C
choices.text: CHS is autosomal dominant; CGD is autosomal recessive

choices.label: D
choices.text: CHS is autosomal recessive; CGD is typically X-linked

choices.label: E
choices.text: CHS is typically X-linked; CGD is autosomal recessive

explanation.summary: LAD-I and CHS are autosomal recessive, whereas CGD is typically X-linked.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in LYST, with fewer than 1000 known cases. Most cases of chronic granulomatous disease are X-linked, meaning the recessive gene for NADPH oxidase is carried on the X chromosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although some CGD cases are autosomal recessive, CGD is typically X-linked.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CHS is autosomal recessive, not X-linked.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CHS is recessive, not dominant, and CGD is typically X-linked rather than autosomal recessive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The patterns are reversed: it is CGD, not CHS, that is typically X-linked.

questions.stem: A cell biologist observes that when a cell's organelles become damaged, lysosomes degrade them so that the resulting amino acids and polysaccharides can be reused to build new molecules. Which of the following terms describes this process?

explanation.summary: Autophagy (self-eating) is the lysosomal breakdown of damaged cellular components so their building blocks can be reused.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vesicles such as lysosomes have functions beyond immunity. In autophagy, lysosomes break down damaged cellular components so that their individual amino acids and polysaccharides can be reused to create new molecules. This is one of the vesicle functions that depends on proper lysosomal trafficking.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Diapedesis is the migration of a leukocyte across the endothelium into tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extravasation is another name for diapedesis, the exit of leukocytes from the vessel.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Margination refers to neutrophils rolling on the endothelium or moving into tissues rather than circulating freely.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phagocytosis is the ingestion of external material such as pathogens, after which lysosomes fuse with the phagosome; it does not describe recycling of the cell's own components.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old girl with confirmed Chediak-Higashi syndrome has fair skin and sparse silver hair. Which of the following best explains her hypopigmentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tyrosinase mutation prevents melanin synthesis in melanocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells attack melanocytes in the skin and hair follicles

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enlarged melanosomes in melanocytes are not properly transferred to keratinocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Melanocytes fail to migrate into the skin during development

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactive oxygen species from neutrophils destroy melanin in keratinocytes

explanation.summary: In CHS, defective vesicle trafficking produces enlarged melanosomes that cannot be delivered to keratinocytes, causing partial oculocutaneous albinism.
explanation.whyCorrect: Melanin, a pigment found in skin, hair, and retina, is distributed by vesicles. Because LYST regulates vesicle trafficking and fusion, the melanocytes of CHS patients contain enlarged pigment granules (melanosomes) that cannot be properly transferred to keratinocytes or epithelial cells. The resulting hypopigmentation varies, but most patients have fair skin and sparse light blond, gray, silver, or white hair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Melanin is synthesized in CHS (the melanosomes are enlarged, not empty); the defect is in LYST-dependent trafficking, not tyrosinase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CHS albinism is a vesicle-trafficking defect, not an autoimmune attack; cytotoxic T cells in CHS are themselves impaired by defective lysosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Melanocytes are present in CHS; the problem is delivery of their pigment granules, not their migration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive oxygen species are generated inside neutrophil phagolysosomes to kill microbes and play no role in the albinism of CHS.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with Chediak-Higashi syndrome received a hematopoietic stem cell transplant at age 3, after which his infections and bleeding resolved and his blood counts normalized. Over the past 2 years he has developed progressive loss of balance, tremor, peripheral neuropathy, and declining cognitive ability. Which of the following best explains why the transplant did not prevent these new problems?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic Staphylococcus aureus infection has spread to the central nervous system

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor lymphocytes are attacking his peripheral nerves as graft-versus-host disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has developed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis infiltrating the nervous system

choices.label: D
choices.text: HSCT replaces marrow-derived cells but cannot replace neurons with defective vesicle trafficking

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transplanted graft has failed and his own defective leukocytes have returned

explanation.summary: Neurologic defects in CHS arise from impaired vesicle trafficking in neurons, which HSCT cannot correct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood cells begin their lives in the bone marrow, so HSCT can replace defective platelets, erythrocytes, and leukocytes; it cannot replace defective neurons. Most CHS patients who receive HSCT and live to adulthood develop neurological defects by their early 20s that worsen over time, including loss of balance, tremors, peripheral neuropathy, and lower cognitive ability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: S. aureus infections are the most common infections in untreated CHS, but his infection risk was corrected by transplant and the picture is a progressive neurodegenerative one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes the neurologic course of CHS to intrinsic neuronal vesicle-trafficking defects, not to donor-versus-host attack on nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLH occurs in more than 80% of patients without HSCT and presents as a hyper-inflammatory state with pancytopenia, not an isolated slowly progressive neurologic syndrome in a transplanted patient with normal counts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: His infections and bleeding remain resolved with normal counts, indicating the graft is functioning; the neurologic decline is expected even with a successful graft.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy with Chediak-Higashi syndrome has had, in addition to repeated Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, several unusually severe and prolonged viral illnesses. Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to viral infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent selectin ligands on circulating lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defective lysosomes in cytotoxic T cells and NK cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of neutrophils to undergo diapedesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lack of NADPH oxidase in phagocytes

explanation.summary: In CHS the lysosomes of neutrophils, cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells are all defective, impairing responses to both bacterial and viral infections.
explanation.whyCorrect: LYST mutations disrupt lysosome trafficking and fusion in multiple cell types. Because the lysosomes of neutrophils, cytotoxic T cells, and NK cells are all defective in CHS, the response to both bacterial and viral infections is impaired. S. aureus infections are the most common, but the cytotoxic-cell defect explains the viral susceptibility.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Selectin ligands (sialyl-Lewis X) are not affected in CHS; the disease is a vesicle-trafficking disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Terminal complement deficiency causes recurrent Neisseria infections and is a separate innate IEI.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Failure of diapedesis is the LAD-I defect; CHS neutrophils reach tissue and phagocytize but cannot deliver lysosomal contents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NADPH oxidase deficiency is the CGD defect and leads to catalase-positive bacterial and fungal infections, not the viral susceptibility described.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl with partial albinism and recurrent pyogenic infections has a peripheral blood smear showing giant inclusion bodies in her neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Genetic sequencing identifies a previously unreported variant in the LYST gene. Which of the following best describes the challenge in interpreting this genetic result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Genetic testing is uninformative in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome because the disorder arises sporadically and is not inherited

choices.label: B
choices.text: LYST has a single known disease-causing mutation, so any variant other than that one must be benign and cannot explain the phenotype

choices.label: C
choices.text: LYST is a large gene with many possible causative mutations, so pathogenic variants can be hard to distinguish from normal variation

choices.label: D
choices.text: LYST variants are only clinically meaningful when they are inherited on the X chromosome from a carrier mother

choices.label: E
choices.text: The blood smear findings are nonspecific in this disorder, so only the genetic result can establish the diagnosis

explanation.summary: Genetic screening is the definitive test for CHS, but the large LYST gene and its many causative mutations make pathogenic variants hard to separate from normal variation.
explanation.whyCorrect: CHS is diagnosed with a combination of blood smear and genetic testing. Although genetic screening is the definitive test, the LYST gene is large and multiple mutations can cause CHS, so differentiating between mutations that cause CHS and normal variations of the LYST gene can be difficult. The smear showing giant inclusion bodies in granulocytes strongly supports the diagnosis in this child.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CHS is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder, and genetic testing is part of its diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CHS results from multiple different LYST mutations, not a single defined mutation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LYST is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, not on the X chromosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Giant inclusion bodies in neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils are a classic smear finding for CHS; the smear is informative, not nonspecific.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with Chediak-Higashi syndrome is awaiting a hematopoietic stem cell transplant. He is on prophylactic antibiotics but continues to have frequent bacterial infections, and his laboratory results show a persistently low absolute neutrophil count. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy to correct this laboratory abnormality?

explanation.summary: In CHS, G-CSF may be given to correct neutropenia and decrease infections while awaiting HSCT.
explanation.whyCorrect: CHS is treated with prophylactic antibiotics and aggressive therapy for acute bacterial infections. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) may be given to correct neutropenia and decrease infection. HSCT remains the only treatment capable of replacing the defective leukocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Platelet transfusion addresses bleeding from defective platelet granules, not a low neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The problem is neutropenia with bacterial infections; antifungal prophylaxis does not correct the neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granuloma removal is a CGD intervention (especially in the respiratory tract); CHS is not characterized by granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IFN-gamma is used in moderate chronic granulomatous disease, not to raise neutrophil counts in CHS.

questions.stem: Within a neutrophil phagolysosome, NADPH oxidase has just generated superoxide from molecular oxygen. Which of the following enzymes catalyzes the next step, converting superoxide into hydrogen peroxide?

explanation.summary: In the respiratory burst, superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, which myeloperoxidase then uses to make hypochlorite.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxygen-dependent killing begins with NADPH oxidase generating superoxide from O2. Superoxide dismutase then converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, and myeloperoxidase combines hydrogen peroxide with chloride to form hypochlorite (bleach), which destroys bacteria in the phagolysosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase breaks hydrogen peroxide down into water and oxygen; in the brick's pathway it is a bacterial enzyme that protects microbes rather than a step in killing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LYST regulates lysosome trafficking and fusion; it is not an enzyme of the respiratory burst.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloperoxidase acts one step later, converting hydrogen peroxide and chloride into hypochlorite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NADPH oxidase performs the first step (O2 to superoxide), which has already occurred in this scenario.

questions.stem: A laboratory without flow cytometry evaluates a 3-year-old boy with recurrent Serratia and Aspergillus infections using an older assay in which stimulated neutrophils are incubated with a colorless compound. In healthy control cells the compound is converted to a blue product. Which of the following results is expected from this patient's neutrophils if he has chronic granulomatous disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells fail to turn blue because superoxide is not generated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells fluoresce because rhodamine is produced

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cells turn blue at the normal rate because myeloperoxidase is intact

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cells turn blue only after bacterial catalase is added

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cells turn deep blue because hydrogen peroxide accumulates

explanation.summary: In the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test, CGD neutrophils fail to turn the colorless compound blue because they lack NADPH oxidase.
explanation.whyCorrect: The older test for NADPH oxidase function measures the oxidation of a colorless compound, nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT), to a blue compound and quantifies the amount of blue dye produced. Because CGD phagocytes lack functional NADPH oxidase and cannot begin the oxidative burst, the compound stays colorless.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fluorescent rhodamine is the readout of the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry test, not the NBT test, and CGD cells produce little to none.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although myeloperoxidase is intact in CGD, the NBT test depends on NADPH oxidase activity, which is absent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacterial catalase destroys hydrogen peroxide and protects microbes; it would not restore color change in the assay.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Without NADPH oxidase, no superoxide is made, so hydrogen peroxide is not produced by the neutrophil and no blue product forms.

questions.stem: Two unrelated patients each carry one X chromosome bearing a mutation in the X-linked NADPH oxidase gene: a 6-year-old with Turner syndrome (45,X) and a 6-year-old with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). Neither has other affected relatives. Which of the following statements about their risk of chronic granulomatous disease is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both patients are equally likely to be affected because each carries one mutant allele

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neither patient can be affected because CGD requires two mutant alleles

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 45,X patient is more likely to be affected because her only X chromosome carries the mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 47,XXY patient is more likely to be affected because extra X chromosomes amplify the defect

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 47,XXY patient is more likely to be affected because Klinefelter patients are phenotypically male

explanation.summary: For an X-linked recessive gene, people with a single X chromosome (XY or XO) are far more likely to be affected than those with two X chromosomes (XX or XXY).
explanation.whyCorrect: Most cases of CGD are X-linked, meaning the gene is recessive and encoded on the X chromosome. Those with only one X chromosome (e.g., XY and XO people) are much more likely than those with two X chromosomes (e.g., XX and XXY people) to be affected by a deficiency in a gene carried on the X chromosome, because the 47,XXY patient has a second X that can supply a normal copy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are not equally likely: the XO patient has no second X to compensate, whereas the XXY patient does.
whyWrongByChoice.B: For an X-linked recessive gene, a single mutant allele on a lone X chromosome is sufficient to cause disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Extra X chromosomes provide additional normal copies of the gene and reduce, rather than amplify, the likelihood of disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phenotypic sex is not what matters; the number of X chromosomes is. The XXY patient has a second X chromosome that can carry a normal allele.

questions.stem: A pediatric immunologist notes that patients with chronic granulomatous disease develop both abscesses and granulomas more often than healthy children, yet teaches trainees that the increase in granulomas is the more striking finding. Which of the following best explains why the rise in granulomas stands out?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abscesses are already common in healthy people, whereas granulomas are otherwise rare

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abscesses do not form in CGD because its neutrophils cannot migrate into the infected tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Granulomas are the only lesions that respond to IFN-gamma therapy in CGD

choices.label: D
choices.text: Granulomas form only when catalase-positive fungi are present in the tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Granulomas in CGD are caused by overactivity of the NADPH oxidase complex

explanation.summary: Because abscesses are far more prevalent than granulomas in healthy people, the disproportionate increase in granulomas in CGD is striking.
explanation.whyCorrect: When CGD phagocytes cannot clear an infection, the immune system walls it off in an abscess or a granuloma, both of which are encapsulated structures that prevent dissemination. People with CGD are at increased risk of both, but because abscesses are significantly more prevalent in healthy people than granulomas, the increase in granulomas is the more striking change.

whyWrongByChoice.B: In CGD neutrophils enter tissue normally (unlike LAD-I); the defect is in killing, and abscesses do form.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IFN-gamma is used in moderate CGD to reduce infections; the brick does not describe it as a granuloma-specific treatment, and granulomas may require surgical removal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Granulomas wall off infections that cannot be cleared, whether bacterial or fungal; they are not exclusive to fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CGD is caused by deficient, not overactive, NADPH oxidase.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with moderate chronic granulomatous disease confirmed by DHR testing is being monitored closely, with infections treated promptly when they arise. His physician wishes to add a cytokine therapy to reduce the frequency of infections. Which of the following is the most appropriate agent?

explanation.summary: Moderate CGD may be treated with type II interferon (IFN-gamma) or granulocyte transfusions, while HSCT is the only cure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Currently the only cure for CGD is HSCT. Patients with moderate forms of the disease are usually monitored for infections and treated quickly, although they may be treated with type II interferons (IFN-gamma) or granulocyte transfusions to reduce infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: G-CSF is used in Chediak-Higashi syndrome to correct neutropenia; CGD patients do not lack neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-1 increases vascular permeability and adhesion molecule expression; it is not used therapeutically in CGD.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-8 increases LFA-1 affinity for ICAMs during neutrophil recruitment; it is not a therapy for CGD.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TNF-alpha increases endothelial ICAM expression during inflammation and is not a CGD treatment.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy with chronic granulomatous disease develops progressive cough and wheezing. Imaging shows a mass narrowing a mainstem bronchus, and biopsy confirms a granuloma with fungal elements on silver staining. Despite antimicrobial therapy the obstruction persists. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to relieve the airway obstruction?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surgical removal of the obstructing lesion

explanation.summary: Granulomas in CGD must occasionally be removed, especially when they involve the respiratory tract.
explanation.whyCorrect: In CGD, infections that cannot be cleared are walled off in granulomas, and lung granulomas containing fungus are a classic finding. The brick notes that granulomas must occasionally be removed, especially in the respiratory tract, because an encapsulated lesion obstructing the airway will not resolve with antimicrobial therapy alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD18 flow cytometry diagnoses LAD-I; this patient already has a confirmed diagnosis of CGD.
whyWrongByChoice.B: G-CSF corrects neutropenia in CHS; it does not shrink an established granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NBT testing is a diagnostic assay for NADPH oxidase function and would not treat the obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibiotic prophylaxis helps prevent new infections but cannot remove an obstructing encapsulated lesion.
